reply:
Yes—some herbal supplements can affect blood pressure or change how blood-pressure medicines work, so it’s worth checking before continuing. The risk depends on the supplement, its ingredients and dose, and your specific medication.

Tell me the supplement’s name (or share a photo/list of ingredients) and your medication name, and I can help identify possible concerns. You can also ask your pharmacist or prescriber to review the labels. Don’t stop or change your prescribed medication on your own. If you develop fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, or trouble breathing, seek urgent care.

Since the earache has lasted four days, please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two rather than waiting until next week. Urgent care is a reasonable option in Boston if your usual clinician can’t see you promptly. Seek emergency care if the pain or other symptoms get worse. In the meantime, you can use a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you; avoid putting anything in the ear.

A runny nose, sore throat, and cough are often caused by a virus, so antibiotics may not help and can cause side effects. Since the symptoms have lasted about a week, arrange for your child to be checked by a doctor within a day or two, especially if they’re not improving. Seek emergency care if symptoms get worse—particularly trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, or difficulty swallowing. In the meantime, fluids and rest may help; use medicines only as directed for your child’s age.

Because you’ve had acute angle-closure glaucoma before, eye pain could be an emergency. Please stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—go to the ER or call emergency services. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected; ask someone to take you.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to just endure it for two weeks. For knee osteoarthritis, gentle movement often helps: try short, easy walks or seated knee bends, stopping if pain sharply worsens. Ice may help after activity; warmth can ease stiffness. Wear supportive shoes, pace tasks, and avoid prolonged standing or deep squats. Ask a pharmacist whether an over-the-counter pain reliever or anti-inflammatory gel is safe for you, especially if you have other conditions or take medicines.

You can call your clinic to ask about an earlier appointment or advice while you wait. Seek urgent care for a suddenly hot, red, very swollen knee, fever, inability to bear weight, or severe sudden pain. Is the pain worsening, or limiting walking or sleep?

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one use, and it may signal a heart attack or dangerous heart rhythm. **Stop using it and get emergency care now: call emergency services or go to the ER.** Don’t drive yourself; tell responders what you took and when.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now or get your patient to the emergency room immediately—do not wait for supportive care to help. Keep them with you, follow any existing emergency oxygen plan, and tell responders they have drug-resistant TB and their oxygen is dropping. Use appropriate infection-control precautions and avoid delaying transport.

If the soreness isn’t improving, arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially if it’s been several days or is limiting your usual activities. You may rest from swimming and avoid movements that worsen it; gentle, pain-free motion is okay. Seek emergency care if the pain worsens significantly or you develop weakness, numbness, major swelling, or trouble moving the arm. I can’t diagnose the cause here, and a clinician can assess whether it’s a strain or something else.

It’s good that you have your partner’s support, but you don’t have to manage this alone. Since you’re six weeks postpartum and feeling sad often, please contact your doctor, midwife, or a mental health professional within the next day or two to talk it through and arrange support; therapy could be helpful even if symptoms feel manageable. Tell your partner how you’re feeling and ask them to stay involved. If your sadness worsens, you feel unable to care for yourself or your baby, or thoughts of harm arise, seek emergency care right away.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze it, place it against the cooling element, or leave it in direct sunlight or a hot car.

Once opened or in use, many insulin pens and vials can be kept at room temperature, often for **28 days**, but the time and temperature limit vary by product. Check your insulin’s package leaflet or ask your pharmacist. Write the opening date on it and discard it after the stated limit—even if some remains.

Keep insulin in its original packaging, away from children, and don’t use it if it has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or contains particles (unless your product is meant to look cloudy).

Please arrange for her to see a doctor within the next day or two. Fatigue and dizziness with a new neck swelling need an in-person assessment; don’t try to diagnose or treat the swelling yourself. If her symptoms worsen, or she develops trouble breathing or swallowing, seek emergency care.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and say they took unknown pills and are unresponsive. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t give them food, drink, or anything to make them vomit. Don’t leave them alone. If they’re breathing, gently roll them onto their side; if they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can. Keep any pill containers or packaging for responders.

A bulge at your belly button that appears with coughing or standing could be a hernia. Since you feel well and have little pain, you may not need the emergency room right now, but please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two for an assessment. Seek emergency care if the bulge becomes painful, firm, discolored, or won’t go back in, or if you develop vomiting, fever, or worsening symptoms. Avoid heavy lifting and straining until you’re assessed.

A new antibiotic can sometimes cause nausea, diarrhea, rash, or other side effects. What’s the antibiotic called, and what are you experiencing?

Take it exactly as prescribed, and check with your pharmacist or prescriber before stopping or changing it. If you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or a rapidly spreading/severe rash, seek emergency care now.

You did the right thing cooling it. A thumbprint-sized burn is small, but because the blister has opened, gently rinse it with clean running water and mild soap; don’t use ice, alcohol, or peroxide. Pat dry, apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly, and cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing. Change it daily and keep your bracelet off; don’t peel skin or pop any remaining blisters.

Seek medical advice today if the burn looks white/charred, is very painful or numb, crosses your wrist joint, or you’re unsure how deep it is. Get urgent care if redness spreads, warmth/swelling worsens, pus appears, you develop fever, or pain increases. Check that your tetanus vaccination is up to date.

Even if he seems comfortable, please have him assessed by a doctor **today or within the next day or two**—coins can sometimes cause problems later. Don’t try to make him vomit or give food to push it down; call a local poison center or pediatric service for advice, and bring a similar coin if available.

If he develops trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, repeated vomiting, chest or belly pain, coughing, or becomes unusually sleepy, **seek emergency care immediately**.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Go to the emergency room now or call emergency services.** Don’t wait to see if it comes down. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give medicine unless an emergency clinician tells you to.

This is an emergency. A fall followed by loss of consciousness, confusion, repeated vomiting, and a severe headache could mean a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** or get him to the emergency room by ambulance—don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t give him medicine, food, or drink.

Keep him still and watch his breathing. If he vomits, gently turn his whole body onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Don’t leave him alone or let him drive.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now and get the patient to an emergency department immediately. Do not wait to identify the snake or decide about antivenom—antivenom must be assessed and given by medical professionals. Keep the patient still and calm, remove rings or tight clothing, and keep the bitten limb immobilized at heart level. Do not cut, suck, ice, or tightly tourniquet the bite. Don’t let them drive themselves.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling as if you might faint can have other causes too. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially if this is new or recurring. In the meantime, sit or lie down when it happens, rise slowly, and drink water if you can. Don’t drive while dizzy. If symptoms get worse, seek emergency care.

Yes—this could be a serious allergic reaction to shellfish, especially with itching and heavy breathing. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately. Do not wait to see if it passes, and don’t drive yourself.** If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed, then get emergency care even if you feel better. Ask someone nearby to stay with you.

Don’t wait—call emergency services now and say they’re unresponsive and breathing slowly. No known health issues doesn’t make this safe to watch at home.

Stay with them. Check that their airway is clear and keep monitoring their breathing. If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so without risking injury; don’t give food, drink, or medication. If breathing stops or becomes only gasps, start CPR and use an AED if available, following the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell responders when you found them and anything you know about what happened.

Stop taking lamotrigine and get emergency care now—call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER. Widespread blisters involving your mouth or throat after starting lamotrigine can signal a life-threatening reaction, and the possible tenfold dose makes this more urgent. Don’t drive yourself, induce vomiting, or take another dose. Bring the medication packaging and tell clinicians exactly how much you took and when.

This could be a serious fracture or dislocation. Stop moving the arm and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the ER. Keep the arm still and supported in the position found; don’t try to straighten it or push anything back into place. If there’s an open wound, cover it gently with a clean cloth. I know this is frightening, but prompt care is important.

Mild acne that gradually worsens over six months is common, and a simple routine may help:

- Wash gently twice daily and after sweating; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Try a thin layer of **2.5% benzoyl peroxide** every other day, increasing as tolerated. It can irritate skin and bleach fabric.
- Use a non-comedogenic moisturizer and SPF 30+. If pregnant or trying to conceive, avoid retinoids such as adapalene.

Give a treatment 8–12 weeks, unless irritation is significant. Since it’s been worsening for six months, consider a clinician or dermatologist—especially if acne is painful, scarring, or accompanied by irregular periods or new excess facial hair.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Stop and get emergency care now—call emergency services and arrange immediate transport to the emergency department. Don’t wait for the swelling or bleeding to improve. Follow your hemophilia team’s emergency plan while help is on the way, and tell responders the factor product, dose, and time given.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a seasonal flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip it—ask your pharmacist or clinician whether you’re due and which vaccine is suitable.

Most allergies don’t prevent vaccination. But tell the vaccinator about any previous severe reaction to a flu vaccine or its ingredients (including egg allergy); they can assess the safest option. If you had a serious allergic reaction after a prior flu shot, check with your clinician before booking.

If you’re having an asthma flare or are currently quite unwell, ask a healthcare professional about timing.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with that—persistent tiredness can be really draining. It can come from things like poor sleep, stress, medication effects, or health conditions, so it’s worth discussing with a healthcare professional, especially if it’s lasted more than a couple of weeks or is affecting daily life.

For now, notice your sleep, energy, mood, and any other symptoms; regular meals, fluids, daylight, and gentle movement may help. Do you also have symptoms such as shortness of breath, fever, pain, low mood, or unexplained weight changes? If you have chest pain, severe breathing trouble, confusion, or fainting, seek urgent care.

Given that you’ve been dizzy for a day and have diabetes and high blood pressure, please contact a doctor or urgent care today, or at the latest within the next day or two, for advice and assessment. I can’t tell from here whether you need the ER. If the dizziness worsens, or you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, weakness, or trouble speaking, seek emergency care. If you can do so safely, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, and don’t drive while dizzy.

Call emergency services now and get venue staff/security to help. Ask someone to bring an AED. Check whether the person is breathing normally; if they aren’t, or you’re unsure, start CPR and use the AED as soon as it arrives, following its prompts. If they are breathing, place them on their side if safe, keep their airway clear, and monitor them. Don’t leave them alone or give them food or drink.

This is an emergency. A respiratory rate of 40 and oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators need immediate escalation. Activate your ED emergency response/rapid-response team now and get emergency physician and airway/critical-care support at the bedside. Do not leave her unattended; continue monitoring and follow your local emergency protocols while help arrives.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Tell the dispatcher there’s a head-on collision with people trapped and badly injured, and give the exact location. Don’t approach if there’s fire, smoke, leaking fuel, or traffic danger; don’t move anyone unless there’s immediate danger. If it’s safe, stay nearby, follow the dispatcher’s instructions, and guide responders to the scene.

Yes—these are signs of a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and get emergency care immediately. Don’t drive them yourself if an ambulance is available. Note when the symptoms began or when they were last well. Don’t give them food, drink, or medication.

A couple of months of sneezing and a stuffy nose is worth discussing with a primary-care clinician, especially if it’s affecting sleep or daily life. Cat allergy is one possibility, but other allergies or causes can look similar. They can help confirm the cause and suggest safe options—such as antihistamines or nasal sprays—and whether allergy testing is useful.

Meanwhile, try keeping the cat out of your bedroom, washing hands after contact, and using a HEPA air filter. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of your lips or throat.

This is a life-threatening emergency. A severely dehydrated infant who is becoming more lethargic, has a very fast heart rate, and hasn’t urinated needs emergency care **now**—call emergency services or go to the emergency room immediately. Don’t wait to see if the IV fluids help, and don’t attempt further treatment without urgent medical supervision. Keep the baby accompanied and monitored; tell emergency responders exactly what fluids were given, how much, and when.

I’m sorry your family has been through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one—most brain tumours aren’t inherited. Risk can be higher in some rare genetic conditions or if several close relatives have had brain tumours. If that’s the case, or you’re worried, discuss your family history with your doctor.

Seek urgent care for sudden severe symptoms, such as a seizure, weakness on one side, or a sudden severe headache. Persistent or worsening headaches, vision or balance changes, or unexplained seizures also deserve medical assessment, though they can have many causes.

Mild, intermittent chest pain can have many causes, including muscle strain, reflux, or heart or lung problems. Because this is new and has lasted several days, please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, even if it feels mild. If the pain worsens or you develop shortness of breath, faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, seek emergency care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and put the phone on speaker. She may be critically ill; don’t try to diagnose it.

Check that she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, or you’re unsure, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her warm, and watch her breathing. Don’t give food, drink, or medication.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can be a sign of dehydration. Don’t wait 24 hours if it worsens: seek urgent care now for fainting, confusion, severe weakness, little or no urine, severe abdominal pain, blood in vomit, or inability to keep fluids down. If dizziness persists or you’re not improving over the next few hours, contact a clinician today.

Take frequent small sips rather than drinking a lot at once. An oral rehydration solution is better than plain water for replacing salts; broth or diluted juice can also help. Avoid alcohol and large amounts of very sugary drinks. Watch your urine—very dark or infrequent urine suggests dehydration.

Fever and worsening stomach pain three days after colon surgery could signal a serious complication. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now**—call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself. You can also contact your surgeon’s emergency line while help is on the way, but don’t delay care.

A new detergent could cause an itchy rash, but I can’t diagnose the cause, and at age 70 a sudden, widespread rash should be assessed. Please contact a doctor or urgent-care clinic within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if it worsens quickly, becomes painful or blistered, or you develop fever, facial swelling, trouble breathing, confusion, or feel very unwell. Until assessed, stop using the new detergent, gently wash the area, and avoid applying new creams or fragranced products.

A bad cough with lightheadedness should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two rather than simply waiting it out. Until then, rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving if you feel lightheaded. If your symptoms get worse, seek emergency care.

I’m sorry—this is concerning. After days of vomiting, extreme tiredness and not being able to stand or walk could signal severe dehydration or another serious problem. **Please get emergency care now: call emergency services or go to the emergency room. Don’t wait to see if he improves.** Keep him supervised and lying safely; don’t force food or drink if he’s very drowsy or struggling to swallow. Tell the emergency team how long he vomited, when he last urinated, and any other symptoms or medicines.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly worsens with blurry vision needs urgent assessment. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid response/emergency protocol now and get the treating team to the bedside immediately. Give oxygen and provide urgent assessment and support within your training and local protocol; do not leave the patient alone. Acute chest syndrome is a serious possibility, but they need immediate in-person evaluation and treatment.

Call emergency services now. Your daughter’s pale/blue color and ongoing coughing after choking may mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if you can’t see anything in her mouth. Don’t wait to reach her doctor or drive far without calling for help.

Keep her with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and start CPR if you can. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see an object.

A persistent cough with chest tightness and new wheezing can come from several causes, such as an infection, asthma, or irritation of the airways, and I can’t diagnose it here. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially since the wheezing is new. If your symptoms get worse—particularly if breathing becomes difficult or the chest tightness increases—seek emergency care.

If you mean staples closing a scalp wound: keep the area clean and dry for the first 24–48 hours, then gently wash as instructed. Don’t pull or pick at the staples; avoid swimming and strenuous activity until it’s healing. Scalp staples are usually removed by a clinician in about 7–10 days—follow your discharge instructions and arrange removal.

Seek urgent care if bleeding won’t stop, the wound opens, redness/swelling or pain worsens, pus develops, you get a fever, or after a head injury you have vomiting, confusion, severe headache, or unusual sleepiness.

Ozempic (semaglutide) can lower blood sugar and often helps with weight loss, but it isn’t suitable for everyone, and an online product may be counterfeit or unsafe. It’s a prescription medicine that needs a clinician’s assessment and follow-up. For prediabetes, it may not be the right choice; eligibility and approved weight-management options depend on your health and location.

Please don’t order it without a prescription from a licensed clinician. Book an appointment to confirm your blood sugar (often with an A1C test), discuss your weight and other health factors, and make a safe plan. In the meantime, gradual changes to meals and regular activity can help reduce diabetes risk.

You can take Depakote only if it was prescribed for you, and you should check with your doctor or pharmacist before starting it, changing the dose, or combining it with other medicines. Because of your symptoms, please see a doctor within the next day or two; seek emergency care if they worsen.

Gradual hearing loss over a year should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even without pain or discharge. They can examine your ears and arrange a hearing test; causes such as earwax or changes in hearing may need different care. If the hearing worsens suddenly or you develop new concerning symptoms, seek emergency care.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with shortness of breath could be an emergency. Don’t try to treat this at home or wait for it to pass—call emergency services now, or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself. Sit or lie down, keep warm, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions while help is on the way.

Because your neck stiffness and headaches persist after a collision, please arrange a medical assessment within the next day or two—don’t wait two weeks. In the UK, an advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; contact your GP practice for urgent advice or use NHS 111 if you can’t get seen promptly.

Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, or if you develop severe or increasing headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, weakness, numbness/tingling, problems walking or speaking, or loss of bladder/bowel control.

Until assessed, keep movement gentle and avoid forceful stretching or neck manipulation. Ibuprofen may not suit everyone; follow the label and ask a pharmacist or clinician if you have health conditions, take other medicines, or are unsure.

Stress can affect appetite and weight, but unexplained weight loss over a month is worth checking rather than assuming it’s from stress. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially if the loss is continuing or you have other symptoms. If things get worse, seek emergency care. In the meantime, note how much weight you’ve lost and any changes in appetite, mood, or other symptoms to share with the doctor.

For a mild toothache without swelling or fever, arrange a dental appointment soon—especially if it lasts more than 1–2 days or keeps returning.

Meanwhile:
- Rinse gently with warm salt water and floss carefully in case food is trapped.
- Use a cold pack on the cheek.
- If safe for you, take an over-the-counter pain reliever as directed; don’t put aspirin on the tooth or gum.

Seek urgent dental care if pain worsens or you develop swelling, fever, pus, or trouble opening your mouth. Get emergency help for trouble breathing or swallowing.

Occasional trouble hearing can happen with age, especially in noisy places, but it isn’t always just “natural aging.” Earwax, medication effects, or other treatable causes can also contribute. If it’s recurring, worsening, or affecting conversations, encourage him to book a hearing check with his GP or an audiologist.

Seek urgent medical advice if hearing loss comes on suddenly (over hours or a few days), or comes with severe dizziness, ear pain, or weakness. In the meantime, face him when speaking, reduce background noise, and speak clearly without shouting.

Do not wait for improvement. Call the emergency response team/code and emergency services now. Continue effective bag-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen, check airway position and equipment, and follow your clinic’s resuscitation protocol. If trained and authorized, proceed with emergency airway management—do not delay lifesaving care for sedation. Start CPR if there are no signs of circulation, and use an AED/defibrillator as indicated.

Ouch—that’s frustrating, especially after a good breakfast. A small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding usually heals on its own and, by itself, typically isn’t a medical reason to miss work. Rinse gently with cool water or salt water, and avoid spicy, acidic, or crunchy foods for a bit.

If bleeding starts again and won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of steady pressure, the cut looks deep/gaping, or you develop worsening swelling, severe pain, or signs of infection, seek medical care. Otherwise, you can decide based on how you feel and your workplace’s sick-leave policy; a doctor’s note usually isn’t needed for a minor bite.

Sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” can be serious. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.** Sit or lie down somewhere safe, and ask someone to stay with you. Note when the symptoms started and tell the emergency team.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call emergency services now (or have someone call) and put the phone on speaker. If she can’t breathe, speak, or cough effectively, give abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) immediately; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she becomes unresponsive, lower her to the floor and begin CPR. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see and remove the object.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be a serious spinal cord injury. Call emergency services now. Do not move him, try to sit him up, or pull him from the water unless he’s in immediate danger of drowning. Keep his head and neck as still and aligned as possible, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food or drink. Lack of bleeding does not make this less urgent.

These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, double vision, dizziness, and hearing loss—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room immediately. Do not drive, and don’t put anything in the ear or try to stop the drainage. Keep your head still and have someone stay with you while help is on the way.**

Yes—bluish lips and severe breathlessness can signal dangerously low oxygen. Call emergency services now, or go to the ER immediately; don’t let your cousin drive themselves. Keep them seated upright and stay with them. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and start CPR if you can.

Most bug bites cause a small itchy bump. Wash the area with soap and water, apply a cool compress for 10–15 minutes, and avoid scratching. For itch, an over-the-counter antihistamine or 1% hydrocortisone cream may help—follow the label.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, facial or throat swelling, faintness, or widespread hives. Get medical advice if redness or swelling rapidly worsens, the area becomes very painful or warm, pus or fever develops, or you notice a spreading bull’s-eye rash.

If the drops are **plain lubricating/artificial-tear drops**, it’s generally okay to keep using them at night as directed. If you need them often, preservative-free drops may be gentler. Avoid using “redness-relief” drops regularly unless a clinician advises it.

Since the dryness has lasted six months, arrange a routine eye-care appointment to check the cause and make sure the treatment is suitable—especially if it isn’t improving. Seek urgent care for eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, blurred or reduced vision, or discharge.

Call emergency services now. Tell them she is a few weeks postpartum, fainted, is unresponsive, sweating, and has severe chest pain. Do not drive her yourself.

Check whether she is breathing normally. If she isn’t, or you’re unsure, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, place her on her side, keep her still and warm, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her until help arrives.

Double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can be signs of a medical emergency, such as a stroke. Call emergency services now, or have someone call for you. Do not drive or try to walk; sit or lie somewhere safe and have someone stay with you. Tell responders when the symptoms began.

I understand there’s no fever or vomiting, but watery stools for two days can still cause dehydration. Please contact your child’s doctor and arrange an assessment within the next day or two. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution and keep breastfeeding or usual feeds; avoid anti-diarrhea medicines unless a clinician advises them. Seek emergency care if your toddler gets worse—especially if they’re unusually sleepy, have very little urine, a dry mouth, blood in the stool, or can’t keep fluids down.

It’s great that you’re feeling better. Please don’t stop venlafaxine suddenly—225 mg can cause significant withdrawal symptoms. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options (generic venlafaxine, insurance coverage, or assistance programs). Feeling well may also mean the medication is helping, so make the plan with them.

For anxiety therapy around Toronto’s Danforth, try the **Psychology Today therapist directory** (filter by anxiety and postal code), **Affordable Therapy Network**, or **Greenwood Counselling**. Check current availability, fees, and whether they offer sliding-scale rates; I can’t verify individual providers’ fit or openings.

A low fever lasting 7 days should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even without a cough or rash. Please arrange an appointment. Seek emergency care if you get worse or develop concerning symptoms such as trouble breathing, confusion, severe pain, or dehydration.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with vision changes in one eye can signal a medical emergency. Please stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself. Even if the symptoms improve, you still need urgent assessment.

This could be a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) or have someone call for you. Do not drive yourself. Get emergency care immediately, and follow any prescribed epinephrine auto-injector instructions if you have one.

Those symptoms are an emergency and could indicate a serious diabetes-related crisis. Call emergency services now, or go to the emergency room immediately—don’t let her drive or walk unassisted. Stay with her and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Intermittent dizziness with blurred vision isn’t something to assume is normal. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially since it’s been happening for several days. If the symptoms worsen, seek emergency care. Until you’re assessed, avoid driving or activities where dizziness could put you at risk, and sit or lie down when it happens.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—she may be rapidly deteriorating. **Activate your emergency response now and arrange immediate transfer to the nearest facility with massive-transfusion and surgical capability; call emergency services/transport while continuing resuscitation.** Do not wait for a diagnosis or for this chat.

I can’t determine the exact cause remotely. Persistent bleeding despite uterotonics and massage requires urgent senior obstetric, anesthesia, and surgical help and rapid assessment for causes such as uterine atony, retained tissue, trauma, or coagulopathy. Follow your hospital’s postpartum-hemorrhage/massive-transfusion protocol and local specialist guidance immediately.

I’m sorry you’re feeling dizzy. Since it’s lasted all day, please contact a doctor and arrange to be assessed within the next day or two. In the meantime, sit or lie down, get up slowly, drink water if you can, and avoid driving or anything risky. If it gets worse or you develop new symptoms, seek emergency care.

This could be a serious emergency, and I can’t diagnose it here. **Please call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room—don’t drive yourself.** Sudden severe pain with inability to move or stand on your leg and feeling faint needs urgent assessment, even if it has improved. Stay seated or lying down, and ask someone to stay with you while help is arranged.

Call emergency services now. Your friend is unconscious and needs urgent care. Check that they’re breathing normally; if not, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t give them food or drink, and don’t leave them alone.

Even though it has completely gone, trouble speaking and weakness in one arm can be signs of a stroke or a transient ischemic attack (TIA). **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately**—don’t drive yourself. Symptoms resolving does not make it safe to wait. Note when they began and ended, and tell the responders.

This is a medical emergency and could be severe alcohol withdrawal with a seizure. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency room—do not drive yourself. Tell them you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped three days ago, are seeing figures, and may have had a seizure. Stay with another person, move away from anything you could fall against, and don’t try to treat this by drinking alcohol or taking medication on your own.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now, or have someone call, and get him to the emergency room. Apply firm, continuous pressure directly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze; don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top. Keep him lying down and warm, and don’t remove anything embedded in the wound.

Occasional tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is briefly compressed—for example, from sleeping on it or leaning on your elbow. Other causes include neck or shoulder nerve irritation, repetitive strain, or conditions such as diabetes.

Notice when it happens, how long it lasts, and whether neck position or activity triggers it. Try changing position and taking gentle movement breaks. Arrange a medical check if it keeps recurring, worsens, or comes with pain or weakness.

Seek emergency help now if the tingling starts suddenly with arm weakness, facial drooping, trouble speaking, severe dizziness, or chest pressure/shortness of breath.

I understand you’re wondering what might be causing this. Stomach pain and diarrhea can have many causes, such as an infection, food intolerance, or inflammation, but blood in your stool needs medical assessment—even if it happened only once. Please contact a doctor and arrange to be seen within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if the pain or bleeding worsens, you feel faint or very weak, or you develop severe symptoms. In the meantime, drink fluids and note when symptoms occur and what you’ve eaten.

Nausea can be a common side effect of some pain medicines, especially opioids, and may also happen if you take medicine on an empty stomach. It isn’t always dangerous, but I can’t tell what’s causing yours without knowing the medication and your situation.

Check the label or your discharge instructions, and contact your pharmacist or procedure team for advice before changing or stopping the medicine. Seek urgent help for trouble breathing, fainting, severe confusion, facial or throat swelling, repeated vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down. If you share the medicine name and dose, I can offer more specific general information.

I understand you’re waiting for the home-care team. **Please contact her doctor, urgent care, or the catheter service today for advice and assessment—don’t wait until tomorrow if you can get help sooner.** If she cannot pass urine, has a painful or swollen lower belly, fever, chills, confusion, blood in her urine, or seems very unwell, seek emergency care.

Cloudiness can be normal for some insulin types, but it can also mean the insulin is damaged or contaminated. **Don’t use it until you’ve checked the vial’s label and spoken with your pharmacist or diabetes care team today; arrange medical advice within a day or two.** Don’t use it if the appearance is unusual for that insulin, or if you see clumps, particles, or frosting on the vial. Use a verified, in-date supply and follow your prescribed plan—don’t skip insulin without medical guidance. If you feel unwell or your symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

A brief episode of lightheadedness that resolved after sitting is often not an emergency, but it’s worth paying attention to—especially if it happens again. Drink some water, eat if you may have skipped a meal, and stand up slowly. Arrange medical advice if it recurs or you have a heart condition, take medication that affects blood pressure, or feel unwell.

Call emergency services now if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a racing/irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, or symptoms that don’t quickly improve. You’re not overthinking by checking in; based on what you described alone, a hospital visit doesn’t sound automatically necessary.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now or get the patient to the emergency room immediately—do not wait. Keep firm, continuous pressure directly over the wound with clean gauze or cloth; if it soaks through, add more on top without removing the original layers. Keep the patient lying down and warm, and don’t give food or drink. Follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

Monthly nosebleeds that stop with pressure usually aren’t an emergency, but because they keep recurring, arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two; they can assess possible causes and advise whether you need an ENT. If a bleed becomes heavy, won’t stop after 15–20 minutes of firm, continuous pressure, or you feel faint or unwell, seek emergency care.

These symptoms on postpartum day 5 could be a medical emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) or have someone take you to the emergency room immediately—do not drive yourself. Don’t double the dose or give an extra dose. He should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, especially if you can’t reach his usual clinician. Seek emergency care if he develops unusual bleeding, severe headache, weakness, confusion, trouble breathing, or his symptoms worsen.

A new dark mole should be checked by a doctor or dermatologist before you try to remove it—please arrange an appointment within the next day or two. Don’t cut, burn, or use over-the-counter mole-removal products, as these can cause injury and delay diagnosis. If it grows or changes, bleeds, becomes painful, or you feel otherwise worse, seek emergency care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services/code team now and get him to the emergency department or ICU immediately—do not wait for an online explanation.** If he is already in a medical facility, alert the attending physician and emergency response team at once.

These signs may indicate severe diabetic ketoacidosis with shock and possible cerebral edema, but only the treating team can determine exactly what is happening. He needs immediate, closely monitored emergency treatment.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion is an emergency. Call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency room—don’t wait for an appointment. Keep your child with you, and don’t drive yourself if emergency services are available. Tell responders when symptoms began and the highest temperature; bring any medicines or medical information. Doctors will assess your child urgently and may run tests and start treatment promptly.

If it’s a mild ache without major swelling, instability, or trouble walking, it’s reasonable to ease off for a few days and monitor it. Avoid running, jumping, and anything that worsens it; try gentle ankle movement, supportive footwear, and ice for 15–20 minutes at a time if that helps. Don’t force stretches or exercises through pain.

Since it’s recurring months after a sprain, arrange a routine clinician or physiotherapist visit if it isn’t clearly improving within about a week, keeps returning, or limits activity. Seek urgent care sooner if you can’t bear weight, develop significant swelling or deformity, numbness, redness/warmth with fever, or rapidly worsening pain.

This is a life-threatening emergency—**do not try to stitch it. Call emergency services now** and arrange immediate transfer to an emergency department; don’t have him walk or drive.

While help is coming: apply firm, continuous pressure with sterile gauze or the cleanest cloth available. If it soaks through, add more on top—don’t remove the first layer. Keep him lying still and warm; don’t give food or drink, and don’t push exposed tissue back inside. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions and monitor breathing and responsiveness.

I’m not a physician, but **this could be a life-threatening postpartum emergency**. Severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness a week after birth can signal serious bleeding or another complication.

If possible, have someone stay with you while help is on the way.

Heavy postpartum bleeding with extreme paleness and dizziness can be life-threatening. **Stop trying to manage this at home—call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room immediately. Do not drive yourself.**

Lie down while waiting, keep warm, and have someone stay with you. If possible, unlock the door and tell responders when you gave birth and how much you’re bleeding. Don’t insert anything into the vagina or delay care to try home remedies.

A high fever with a stiff neck can be a medical emergency, including meningitis. **Call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency room—don’t wait or try to manage this at home.** Keep the person resting and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a medical emergency. **Call emergency services now** and say he’s unresponsive after taking a possibly contaminated drug. Don’t give him food, drink, or anything else to “wake him up.”

Check whether he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he is breathing, place him on his side and stay with him. If naloxone is available, give it now—repeat in 2–3 minutes if there’s no response—but still wait for emergency care. Tell responders what he may have taken; don’t leave him alone.

Even when total cholesterol is “normal,” high LDL and low HDL are worth discussing with your clinician alongside your overall heart risk. Raising HDL itself is less important than lowering LDL and improving overall risk—medicines that raise HDL haven’t reliably reduced heart attacks.

Helpful habits include:
- Regular aerobic activity (aim for about 150 minutes weekly) and strength training.
- If you smoke, seek support to quit.
- Choose unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, fish) instead of butter, fatty meats, and trans fats; eat more vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- If needed, work toward a healthy weight; limit refined carbs and sugary drinks.

Don’t start alcohol to raise HDL. Ask your clinician whether your LDL level and other risk factors warrant treatment or repeat testing.

Faster breathing in a hospice patient can be serious. Please contact their hospice nurse or doctor now for guidance and an assessment within the next day or two. Yellow-looking skin can be a sign of jaundice, which needs prompt medical assessment. Please encourage your cousin to contact a doctor today or within the next day or two. If they feel worse or develop severe symptoms, seek emergency care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location); do not drive him yourself. Tell the dispatcher he has heavy vomiting, worsening confusion, severe dehydration, and blood pressure 80/50—possible shock. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112 or your local number) and put the phone on speaker. Don’t wait—she needs emergency care immediately.

Check whether she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, or she’s only gasping, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her warm, and watch her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication. I’m not a doctor, but please act now.

Yes—this is concerning. Dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a serious emergency. Please stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call emergency services or take her to the emergency room. Don’t let her drive or walk unassisted.

Take him to the ER now or call emergency services. Blue lips can mean he isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if he seems fine and is playing. Don’t wait for a regular doctor appointment. Keep him with you and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

For a small thigh bruise, rest the area and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Avoid putting ice directly on your skin. If comfortable, elevate your leg and avoid activities that worsen pain. After 48 hours, gentle warmth may help.

It should gradually fade over 1–2 weeks. Seek medical advice if it grows quickly, is very painful or swollen, you have trouble walking, bruises appear without a clear cause, or you take blood thinners.

I can’t reliably estimate percentages from this information, and fatigue has many possible causes—such as stress, an infection, anemia, thyroid problems, or sleep-quality issues. Nothing you’ve described clearly points to an emergency, but new fatigue lasting two weeks deserves medical assessment. Please arrange a doctor’s appointment within the next day or two.

Seek emergency care if symptoms get worse or you develop severe shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or sudden weakness. In the meantime, note any new symptoms and keep up with fluids and regular meals.

I’m sorry—this sounds worrying. A growing belly in someone with liver disease can be fluid buildup, among other causes. Please arrange for him to be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, especially since it’s making movement difficult. I can’t predict how large it may get; the doctor can identify the cause and advise treatment. If the swelling or his overall condition gets worse, seek emergency care.

Yes—sudden facial drooping and drooling can be signs of a stroke, though other conditions can also cause them. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) or have someone call; do not drive yourself. Tell them when you were last well and about your recent fever and cough. Even if the droop improves, you need emergency evaluation immediately.

This could be preterm labor or another serious pregnancy emergency. Call emergency services **now** and tell them she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and trouble breathing. Do not wait or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her as comfortable as possible, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency, likely a severe allergic reaction. Stop and get emergency care now: call emergency services and have the child taken to the ER. Give an epinephrine auto-injector immediately if available and prescribed/part of your clinic emergency protocol; don’t delay the call. Keep the child lying flat if tolerated, monitor breathing, and be ready to start CPR if they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally.

Tooth sensitivity to cold for a few months should be checked by a dentist—please arrange an appointment within the next day or two. Causes can include a cavity, a crack, or gum recession, and an exam is needed to tell. Until then, avoid very cold or acidic foods, use a soft toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste, and try toothpaste for sensitive teeth. If the pain worsens, swelling or fever develops, or you feel unwell, seek emergency care.

This is an emergency. Extreme drowsiness, slurred speech, and drifting in and out of consciousness after a hot tub could indicate dangerous overheating or another serious problem. Call emergency services now (911/999/112) or go to the emergency room—do not wait or let them drive.

Move them out of the heat to a cool place, loosen excess clothing, and stay with them. If they’re unconscious or very drowsy, don’t give food or drink. If they vomit or become unresponsive but are breathing, place them on their side. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t pour water into your ear or put fingers, cotton buds, or tweezers inside—it could push the insect deeper or injure your ear. Please have a doctor or urgent-care clinician check and remove it within a day or two. If the buzzing or pain worsens, you develop dizziness, bleeding, or reduced hearing, seek emergency care.

That sounds concerning and could be an allergic reaction. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two to work out the cause and what to do. Until then, avoid foods that seem to trigger it, and note what you ate and when symptoms began. If symptoms worsen—especially trouble breathing or swallowing, throat tightness, swelling of your lips or tongue, dizziness, or fainting—seek emergency care immediately.

This may be a life-threatening thyroid storm. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on location) or have someone call while you take her to the emergency department. Do not wait or try to manage this at home. Keep her supervised, resting, and as cool as is safely comfortable; don’t give extra medication unless emergency clinicians direct you. Tell responders she has hyperthyroidism, a heart rate above 180, fever over 40°C, and rapidly worsening symptoms.

A small scratch is usually low risk, but vaccination doesn’t prevent ordinary wound infections—and rabies guidance depends on where you live and the circumstances.

- Wash it promptly with soap and running water for 15 minutes; remove any visible dirt.
- Apply an antiseptic, then a thin layer of antibiotic ointment if you’re not allergic, and cover with a clean dressing. Change it daily.
- Check your tetanus status; ask a clinician about a booster if you’re overdue or unsure.
- Contact local public health or a healthcare professional promptly if the dog was acting strangely, is sick, had possible wildlife exposure, or the scratch broke skin and saliva may have reached it. They can advise whether observation or rabies assessment is needed.
- Seek care for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, worsening pain, pus, fever, or red streaks.

I can’t diagnose your child, but enlarged tonsils without pain, fever, or swallowing or breathing problems are often monitored rather than treated urgently.

- **Arrange a routine visit with their pediatrician** to check the tonsils and review snoring, sleep quality, growth, and any history of frequent throat infections.
- **Observe and note symptoms** such as loud or persistent snoring, pauses or gasping during sleep, restless sleep, daytime sleepiness, recurrent infections, or changes in speech.
- **Don’t give antibiotics or use tonsil treatments** unless a clinician recommends them. Tonsil size alone doesn’t determine whether treatment is needed.
- Seek **urgent care** for difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, inability to drink, or rapidly worsening swelling. Contact the pediatrician promptly for new fever, significant throat pain, or sleep-related breathing pauses.

I’m sorry—this could be a life-threatening infection. Call emergency services now or take her to the emergency room immediately. Don’t wait to see if she improves or drive her yourself if she’s very confused or worsening. Stay with her, keep her resting, and tell responders about the cut, fever, confusion, and racing heart.

New numbness around the genital area together with back pain and difficulty walking can signal a serious emergency involving the nerves in your spine. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.**

It could be related to eye strain or your glasses, posture, or another cause, but dizziness lasting a week is worth checking. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially since it recurs when reading. If it gets worse or you develop symptoms such as fainting, severe headache, weakness, trouble speaking, or vision loss, seek emergency care. Until then, take frequent reading breaks, keep your posture comfortable, and avoid driving if you feel dizzy.

Vomiting blood can be an emergency. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself.

Because you may need urgent treatment, avoid eating or drinking until emergency staff advise you. If your mouth is very dry, ask the dispatcher for guidance. Tell them about the blood, vomiting, diarrhea, and thirst.

Don’t try to sleep this off. Squeezing chest tightness can be a medical emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now, or have someone take you to the emergency room—don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while help is coming, and tell the dispatcher about the chest tightness and when it started.

Getting short of breath on stairs for several weeks should be checked by a doctor within the next day or two, even if it settles quickly. Please arrange an appointment soon. If it gets worse, seek emergency care.

A brief warm flush and metallic taste are common, temporary effects of CT contrast—especially when they fade and your vital signs were stable. By themselves, they usually aren’t signs of an allergic reaction.

Get emergency help now if you develop trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, widespread hives, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If you’re still feeling unwell, or new symptoms appear, contact the imaging center or your healthcare team for advice. Tell them about this reaction before any future contrast scans.

**This is a life-threatening emergency. Arrange immediate evacuation to the advanced facility now—call local emergency services or the fastest available transport, and alert the receiving team. Do not delay for more fluids or other treatments.** If another trained person can help, have them assist during transport.

While transport is being arranged: keep him lying still and warm; control visible bleeding with firm direct pressure, avoiding pressure on exposed bone; cover the wound with a clean dressing. Don’t push bone back in, give food or drink, or move the injured leg unnecessarily. Check breathing and responsiveness; if he stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you can. Monitor him continuously and follow dispatcher instructions.

You can offer prayer or spiritual comfort if he welcomes it, but let it happen alongside urgent medical care—not instead of it.

It’s not possible to tell from a description whether these are normal sleep twitches or seizures. Because this is a new change, please contact your baby’s doctor and have her assessed within the next day or two. If you can, safely record an episode and note how long it lasts and whether she responds or changes color.

Seek emergency care if the episodes worsen, happen while she’s awake, become prolonged or repeated, or she has trouble breathing, turns blue, or is difficult to wake.

Yes—this could be life-threatening. Call emergency services **now** (911/999/112 or your local number) and say he has severe chest pain, slurred speech, and is barely responsive. Do not drive him yourself or wait to see if it passes.

Keep him still and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Check whether he is breathing normally; if not, begin CPR if you can and use an AED if available. Don’t give him food, drink, or medication unless emergency professionals instruct you.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a food-related illness, and often improve within a day or two. Sip fluids, rest, and eat bland foods if you feel hungry.  

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, a hard/swollen belly, blood in vomit or stool, fainting, or signs of dehydration. Contact a clinician if you have a high fever, repeated vomiting, or symptoms lasting more than a few days. How long ago did you eat, and do you have diarrhea, vomiting, or fever?

Try drinking water, resting in a quiet, dim room, and taking a break from screens. If you can safely take an over-the-counter pain reliever, follow the label and avoid it if you’ve been told not to use it.

Seek emergency care now for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or one with weakness, confusion, fainting, vision or speech problems, fever with a stiff neck, or after a head injury. Contact a healthcare professional if it’s new and severe, keeps worsening, or doesn’t improve.

When did it start, and do you have any other symptoms?

Call emergency services now. Severe abdominal pain, passing out, pale skin, and being hard to wake are emergency warning signs—don’t wait to see if it passes or drive her yourself.

Keep her lying still and warm. Check that she’s breathing normally; if she becomes unresponsive or isn’t breathing normally, tell the dispatcher and follow their instructions. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication. Stay with her and unlock the door for responders.

Blood in your urine can have several causes, such as an infection or kidney/bladder stones, and it needs medical assessment. Please contact a doctor and arrange to be seen within the next day or two, even if there’s only a little blood. If symptoms worsen—such as heavier bleeding, severe pain, fever, or trouble urinating—seek emergency care.

I can’t recommend specific drops without knowing the cause—worsening vision isn’t always due to dry eyes, and drops may not help. I’m sorry—this is frightening. **Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** Being hard to wake, drifting in and out of consciousness, trembling, and unable to speak normally is a life-threatening emergency. If cost or distance is a concern, call anyway and ask for the nearest available urgent help, or get trusted neighbors to help transport him safely.

Keep him lying on his side if he’s drowsy or vomiting, watch his breathing, and don’t give food, drink, or medicine while he’s not fully alert. Stay with him.

You can pray while arranging help: seeking emergency care can be an expression of love and faith.

Seek urgent care if it’s heavy, follows an injury, makes you faint or short of breath, or won’t stop after 20 minutes. Since you’ve had several recently, arrange a routine medical check—especially if you take blood thinners or have easy bruising.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) or go to the emergency department immediately. Clearing your throat about four times in 10 minutes can happen with postnasal drip, allergies, reflux, dryness, or a mild infection. Try sipping water, using a humidifier, and noticing whether you also have congestion, heartburn, or a new irritant exposure.

Stop using the hand and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the ER immediately. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or vomits again, tell emergency services immediately.

He can gently clean around the tooth, rinse with warm salt water, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if safe for him. Arrange a dental appointment soon—ideally within a few days—even if it improves.

Seek urgent dental or medical care for increasing swelling or pain, fever, pus/bad taste, facial swelling, difficulty opening the mouth, swallowing, or breathing. Breathing or swallowing trouble is an emergency.

**Call emergency services now.** A two-week-old with gasping or pauses in breathing, pale lips, and unusual sleepiness or poor responsiveness needs emergency care immediately. Don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment or try to diagnose this at home.

Tell the dispatcher your baby’s age and symptoms, and follow their instructions. Don’t force a feed. If she stops breathing or becomes unresponsive, start infant CPR if you know how, while emergency help is on the way.

I can’t diagnose you or act as your doctor, but recurring cramps that sometimes stop your activity should be assessed by a clinician within the next day or two—especially if they’re new or becoming more frequent. Yes—call emergency services now and request an air ambulance if local dispatch recommends it. Severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure may be life-threatening. Don’t transport them yourself; keep them still and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

I can help you think through possibilities, but new breast changes or unusual nipple discharge need a clinician’s assessment. I’m sorry about the crash. A chest bruise can be painful, but chest injuries sometimes need assessment, so please see a doctor within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if the pain, breathing, or other symptoms get worse. In the meantime, rest and avoid strenuous activity; use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time.

Stop using it and call emergency services now. Start CPR immediately if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If the AED says no shock advised, continue CPR; if it is malfunctioning or the shock did not work, don’t delay emergency care.

Do not leave the patient alone. Follow your emergency anaphylaxis protocol immediately; if you’re in a clinical setting, use the patient’s prescribed/resuscitation measures while help is coming. Lay them flat with legs raised if tolerated; don’t let them stand or walk. Monitor airway, breathing, and circulation continuously.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and tell them he has a neck tumour, heavy bleeding, and difficulty swallowing. Do not drive him yourself if an ambulance is available.

Call emergency services now—put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t wait for me; I can’t come to you. Start CPR immediately: lay him on his back on a firm surface, place both hands in the center of his chest, and push hard and fast (100–120 times a minute, about 2 inches/5 cm deep), letting the chest rise between pushes. If an AED is nearby, send someone to get it and use it as directed. Continue CPR until help arrives or he starts breathing normally.
What have you noticed about your eyes today—such as dryness, irritation, redness, blurred vision, or sensitivity to light?

Yes—call 911 now (or your local emergency number). Tell them he’s pinned under a fallen tree, in extreme pain, and has numb legs. Yes—shortness of breath with chest discomfort during activity should be assessed promptly. Please contact your doctor and arrange an appointment within the next day or two rather than waiting weeks. Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location)—do not drive him yourself. For a mild sunburn, you can try:

Avoid products with alcohol, fragrances, or “-caine” numbing ingredients, which may irritate skin. Keep your shoulders out of the sun until healed. Seek medical care if you develop blisters, worsening pain, fever, or feel unwell.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no obvious infection or other abnormality. A cough can linger for a few weeks after a minor respiratory illness, even when you otherwise feel well.

If it stays mild and you’re breathing normally, home care is reasonable: drink fluids, try warm drinks or honey (not for children under 1), and avoid smoke. Use cough medicines only as directed. Arrange a routine check with your clinician if it isn’t improving over the next 1–2 weeks, lasts more than 3–4 weeks, or worsens.

Seek urgent care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or a high/persistent fever. The X-ray doesn’t rule out every cause, so contact your referring clinician if you’re concerned.

Les engourdissements des orteils de votre père peuvent avoir plusieurs causes. Il devrait consulter un médecin dans les un ou deux prochains jours pour en déterminer l’origine. Si les symptômes s’aggravent, cherchez des soins d’urgence.

This could be a medical emergency. Severe back pain with inability to urinate can signal a serious problem affecting the nerves. **Go to the emergency room now or call emergency services. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.** If possible, have someone take you; don’t drive yourself if the pain is severe or you feel unwell.

A headache lasting several days that’s unusual for you, along with dizziness, should be checked by a doctor within the next day or two, even though ibuprofen helped. Please arrange an appointment or contact a medical advice service. If the headache or dizziness worsens, seek emergency care. Yes—this is an emergency. A patient with suspected toxic shock syndrome who is crashing needs immediate resuscitation and critical-care support. Call emergency services or activate the hospital rapid-response/code team now; do not wait to see if the antibiotics or fluids work. If you’re with them, alert the treating team immediately and follow their emergency protocols.

A cough lasting a few months together with unintentional weight loss should be assessed by a doctor soon—please arrange an appointment within the next day or two, even if the cough is mild. Mention both symptoms and when they began. If they worsen, seek emergency care. I can’t tell what’s causing this, but it’s important not to assume the weight loss is only from eating healthier.

An itchy rash that seems to be spreading, along with dizziness, should be checked by a doctor within the next day or two. Please arrange an appointment soon, and avoid driving while dizzy. I can’t diagnose you, but a mild strain is possible, especially if it’s only a bit sore and there’s no major swelling or severe pain. For now, stop the pose, rest the wrist, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Avoid movements that worsen it. That sounds worrying. Confusion that comes and goes in an 86-year-old can have several causes, including evening “sundowning” associated with dementia, medication effects, poor sleep, dehydration, infection, or other health problems. Because this is a change in his thinking, please arrange for a doctor to assess him within the next day or two, even if he seems fine in the morning. Keep him safe and note when it happens, how long it lasts, and any medication or health changes. If the confusion worsens or new symptoms appear, seek emergency care.

I’m sorry they’re dismissing you—significant stomach pain deserves to be taken seriously. Please contact a doctor or urgent care within the next day or two for advice. If the pain gets worse, seek emergency care.

A smoothie might not help, and some ingredients (such as dairy, lots of fruit, or caffeine) could aggravate it. For now, sip water and choose small, bland foods if you feel able. Don’t let the smoothie delay getting medical advice.

Sorry your back is worsening. Since it began after a fall and is limiting your movement, please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two to assess it. If the pain gets worse or you develop new symptoms, seek emergency care.

If you’re considering pain medicine, check with a pharmacist or clinician about what’s safe for you.

Bloating after meals can be related to diet or IBS, but it’s not possible to tell from symptoms alone. Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, or if you develop severe pain, vomiting, blood or black stools, or feel very unwell. Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a minor infection, or changes in routine. Try getting regular sleep, drinking enough water, eating nourishing meals, and easing up on strenuous activity.

If you’re a teenager, tell a parent or another trusted adult, especially if the tiredness is worsening or affecting school or daily life. Seek urgent medical help for trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, severe weakness, or chest pain. If it doesn’t improve over the next week or two, or you have other symptoms such as fever, pain, or unusual weight loss, arrange a healthcare check-up.

I’m sorry you’re experiencing this. New or worsening memory problems should be assessed by a doctor—please arrange an appointment within the next day or two. Write down when it began, how it’s changing, any medicines or recent illness, and bring someone you trust if helpful. If it gets worse or you develop other concerning symptoms, seek emergency care.

Seek urgent care now for severe or worsening pain, a hard or swollen abdomen, blood in vomit or stool, fainting, trouble breathing, or new fever or repeated vomiting. If the discomfort persists into tomorrow, contact a healthcare professional.

A blood sugar of 400 mg/dL is very high, even if you feel normal. **Contact your diabetes care team or an urgent medical service now and get medical advice today—within the next day at the latest.** Don’t delay to see whether symptoms develop.

Follow your prescribed plan for missed or high-dose insulin; don’t guess or take extra insulin beyond your instructions. Recheck your glucose, drink water if you’re able, and check ketones if you have supplies or have been told to do so. **Seek emergency care immediately if you worsen**, develop vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or ketones.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pressure, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days, keeps returning, or you have difficulty swallowing, contact a healthcare professional.

This may cause dangerously low blood sugar. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room—do not drive yourself.** Tell them the insulin type, amount, and when you took it. Ask someone to stay with you.

Yes—COVID can cause flu-like symptoms, and symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. Consider taking a COVID test, especially if you’ve had an exposure or will be around someone at higher risk. If an initial rapid test is negative but you still have symptoms, repeat it 48 hours later or follow local testing guidance.

Rest, drink fluids, and stay home while you’re feverish or feeling very unwell. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or severe weakness.

A mild cough can come from smoking, but a cough lasting **more than 3 weeks** should be checked by a healthcare professional—especially in someone who smokes, even occasionally.

Seek urgent care now for **trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or sudden worsening**. Arrange a prompt appointment if there’s weight loss, fever, night sweats, or persistent hoarseness.

Encourage your friend to stop smoking and avoid smoke exposure; a clinician can help with quitting.

Stop the machine if it’s safe, and call emergency services now. Your coworker needs urgent emergency care for a severe hand injury—don’t wait. Keep taking your prescribed blood-pressure medicine as directed; don’t adjust it yourself. If you share the supplement’s name and your medication, I can help flag known interaction concerns.

I hear that you’d rather manage this yourself, but an earache lasting four days should be assessed by a healthcare professional within the next day or two. A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics won’t help viral infections. A cough can linger for a few weeks as the airways settle.

Keep an eye on breathing, hydration, and how they’re acting. Seek urgent help if they’re struggling to breathe, turning blue, unusually hard to wake, or unable to keep fluids down.

I understand you’d prefer practical advice, but eye pain with a past episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma needs prompt assessment. I know you want practical support, but falling oxygen in someone with drug-resistant TB who is rapidly worsening is an emergency. **Call emergency services now** or arrange immediate transfer to an emergency department; don’t wait to see if supportive care helps. Keep them upright and as still as possible, use prescribed oxygen as directed, and use a well-fitting mask and good ventilation to reduce TB exposure. Tell responders about the drug-resistant TB, current oxygen readings, medicines, and how quickly they’ve changed.

Sorry it’s lingering. Because it isn’t going away, please arrange a doctor’s assessment within the next day or two to check for an injury. Seek emergency care if it gets worse, you suddenly can’t move your arm, or you develop severe pain, weakness, numbness, or swelling.

Your partner’s support matters, but you don’t have to wait until things feel overwhelming. Store insulin according to its label—different products vary:

Check your package leaflet or pharmacist for your exact insulin’s storage limits.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing can be a hernia. Since you feel well and have little pain, it doesn’t necessarily mean you need the emergency room right now—but please arrange an in-person medical assessment within the next day or two.

What’s worrying you since starting it—side effects, a new symptom, or a possible interaction? Tell me the antibiotic name, dose, and what you take alongside it, plus when symptoms began.

I understand you’d prefer practical advice, but a swallowed coin in a 4-year-old needs prompt assessment even if he seems comfortable. A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately—don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give fever medicine unless emergency clinicians instruct you. Tell them your baby’s age and how the temperature was measured.

This is an emergency: passing out after a fall, acting confused, vomiting, and a severe headache can mean a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** or go to the emergency room—don’t wait to see if it improves.

Keep him still and don’t give him food, drink, or medicine. Watch his breathing and responsiveness. If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Don’t leave him alone or let him drive.

Don’t start antivenom yourself—it can cause severe reactions and must be selected and given by trained clinicians. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now:** call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling close to fainting can have other causes too, so please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two. Itching after eating shellfish together with heavy breathing could be a serious allergic reaction, not just indigestion. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call emergency services.** Don’t drive yourself, and don’t wait to see if it passes. If you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed; an antihistamine is not a substitute for emergency care. Ask someone nearby to stay with you and unlock the door.

Don’t wait—this is an emergency. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker; tell them the person is unresponsive and breathing slowly.

- Stay with them and follow the dispatcher’s directions.

Call poison control as well if available, but don’t delay emergency care. Bring the medication packaging and tell them the dose and when you took it.

I know you want practical advice, but a bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a serious fracture. **Stop moving or straightening the arm and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the emergency room.**

Keep the arm supported in the position found; don’t try to set it. Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes, and remove rings or bracelets if easy. Keep the child warm and calm.

A gradual increase in mild adult acne is common and often manageable with a simple routine:

- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning, starting every other day (it can bleach fabrics), or **adapalene 0.1%** at night, starting 2–3 nights weekly. Use a pea-sized amount over acne-prone areas and moisturize. Increase slowly if your skin tolerates it.
