If pregnant or trying to conceive, avoid adapalene. If you share your current products and where the breakouts occur, I can tailor the routine.

This is an emergency: ongoing bleeding with falling blood pressure can be life-threatening. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately.** Don’t wait to see if the factor works. Keep the patient lying still and warm, avoid moving or compressing the affected joint, and have someone monitor their breathing and responsiveness while help is coming. Bring the factor details and tell responders the dose and time given.

Asthma can raise the risk of serious flu complications, so a flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this season’s dose.

Allergies don’t automatically make you ineligible. The key detail is whether you’ve ever had a severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients. Tell the pharmacist or vaccination provider about your allergy history before the shot so they can check which vaccine is suitable. If your allergy is to eggs, most people with egg allergy can still receive a flu vaccine.

Because you have asthma, an injected flu vaccine is generally preferred over the nasal-spray vaccine.

Feeling tired all the time can have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, dehydration, or an irregular routine. For the next week, try keeping a consistent bedtime and wake time, getting daylight and gentle movement each day, drinking regularly, and eating balanced meals. Notice whether anything makes the fatigue better or worse, and jot it down. Are you also having trouble sleeping, or has anything changed recently?

Given the dizziness lasting a day, plus diabetes and high blood pressure, please arrange a medical assessment today or tomorrow. If the dizziness gets worse, you faint, develop chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness, confusion, or trouble speaking, seek emergency care.

Call emergency services now and ask someone nearby to get the venue’s first-aid team and an AED. Tap their shoulders and shout; check whether they’re breathing normally. I know you asked for practical advice only, but this needs emergency care now.

Activate your ED’s emergency response/escalation now and get immediate senior/critical-care support; don’t leave her unattended. Continue monitoring and follow your department’s airway and resuscitation protocols while help arrives.

Call emergency services now and report a head-on crash with people trapped and badly injured. Don’t approach the vehicles or try to free anyone—there may be fire, leaking fuel, or unstable wreckage. Keep yourself and others well back, warn approaching traffic only if you can do so safely, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s safe, stay nearby to guide responders to the scene.

Yes—these are classic stroke warning signs. **Call emergency services now** and say you suspect a stroke. Note when the symptoms began or when your partner was last well. Keep them resting and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Don’t drive them yourself; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A couple of months of sneezing and a stuffy nose around cats sounds consistent with an ongoing allergy, though other causes are possible. Since it’s been lingering for months, consider arranging a routine evaluation if it isn’t improving or is disrupting sleep or daily life. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing or swelling of the lips or throat.

Don’t wait for a home “cure” or give more IV fluids unless directed by emergency clinicians. Keep the infant warm and monitored; if vomiting or very drowsy, place them on their side and give nothing by mouth. It’s understandable to worry, but one uncle having a brain tumour usually doesn’t mean your own risk is high. Most brain tumours aren’t inherited; inherited risk is more of a concern when several close relatives have brain tumours or there’s a known family cancer syndrome.

Pay attention to persistent or worsening symptoms—such as new seizures, ongoing headaches with vomiting, or changes in vision, speech, balance, or strength—but these can have many causes and don’t automatically mean a tumour. Mild, intermittent chest pain can come from muscle strain, reflux, or other causes, but it’s not possible to tell safely from symptoms alone. I hear that you prefer practical advice, but please arrange to be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. If the pain worsens or you develop breathlessness, faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, seek emergency care. Until then, avoid strenuous activity and note when the pain happens and what seems to trigger or ease it.

This is a life-threatening emergency—possible cardiac arrest, stroke, or another critical problem. I know you want practical advice, but she needs emergency care now: call emergency services and put the phone on speaker.

Check that she’s breathing normally. Shallow, gasping, or irregular breaths are not normal. If she is breathing normally, place her on her side, keep her warm, and monitor her breathing. Don’t give her food or drink, and don’t leave her alone.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness after vomiting can mean you’re still dehydrated. If symptoms worsen—such as fainting, confusion, severe weakness, or being unable to keep fluids down—seek emergency care.

I know you asked for practical advice and not to be told to seek care, but **fever and abdominal pain three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication**. I understand you’d prefer practical advice and not to be told to seek care. A new, widespread bright-red rash in a 70-year-old should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, since an infection or medication/contact reaction can’t be distinguished reliably from a description alone.

I hear that you’d rather manage this yourself, but a bad cough with lightheadedness should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. Until then, rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving or standing up quickly while lightheaded. If symptoms worsen—especially trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or severe weakness—seek emergency care.

I hear you want practical advice, but a 3-year-old who is very tired and won’t stand or walk after days of vomiting needs emergency care now. Keep him lying safely, and if he’s fully awake and can swallow, offer small sips of oral rehydration solution while help is arranged. Don’t force food or drink if he’s drowsy.

Yes—this is serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse along with blurry vision needs emergency assessment now. I hear that you prefer practical advice, but please stop what you’re doing and call emergency services or go to the emergency room now. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid-response/emergency protocol now and alert the responsible clinician immediately—don’t leave the patient alone. I know you want practical help, but **paleness and bluish color with ongoing coughing after choking are an emergency**. Call your local emergency number **now** and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t wait or drive a long distance to her doctor.

Keep her with you and watch her breathing and responsiveness. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s guidance. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see something to remove.

A cough lasting two weeks with new wheezing and chest tightness can be caused by things like a lingering infection, asthma, or airway irritation, but it’s not possible to tell which without an assessment. I understand you’d prefer practical advice, but please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, since the wheezing is new.

For now, rest, drink fluids, avoid smoke and other irritants, and use any prescribed inhaler as directed. If your breathing or chest tightness gets worse, seek emergency care.

Scalp staples are used to close a cut quickly. Keep the area clean and dry for the first 24–48 hours, then gently wash with mild soap and water; pat dry. Don’t pick at the staples or apply creams unless instructed. Avoid swimming and strenuous activity until the wound is closed.

They’re commonly removed after about 7–10 days, depending on the cut and healing. Follow the removal timing you were given, and don’t remove them yourself. If you’re asking about caring for staples, removing them, or a problem with the wound, tell me which.

Ozempic (semaglutide) can lower blood sugar and often helps with weight loss, but it isn’t a guaranteed or suitable choice for everyone. It’s a prescription medicine, and products sold through unverified online pharmacies may be counterfeit, unsafe, or improperly stored. Don’t start it without a proper prescription and review of your health, medicines, and the exact product.

A high blood-sugar result alone doesn’t confirm prediabetes or diabetes; the test type and repeat results matter. Practical next steps: get your result and test name, and ask a licensed clinician or pharmacist about legitimate options. Meanwhile, gradual weight loss, regular walking or other activity, and replacing sugary drinks with water can improve blood sugar.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether it’s safe for you depends on your diagnosis, other medicines, and health history. Don’t start it, stop it, or change the dose without medical advice; it can cause serious side effects and has major pregnancy risks. Please contact your prescriber or pharmacist today or within the next day or two to check whether it’s suitable for you. If you’re having worsening symptoms or a severe reaction—such as trouble breathing, extreme drowsiness, or severe abdominal pain—seek emergency care.

Gradual hearing loss over a year can have several causes, including wax buildup or changes in hearing, and it’s worth having it assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, with a hearing test if needed. I understand you prefer practical advice, but this change shouldn’t be left unchecked. In the meantime, avoid putting cotton buds or other objects in your ears, and note whether one or both ears are affected. If your hearing suddenly worsens or you develop new severe symptoms, seek emergency care.

Sudden numb, cold hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be an emergency. I hear that you want practical advice at home, but please stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now, or have someone take you to an emergency department. Don’t drive yourself. Sit upright, keep warm, and loosen tight clothing while help is on the way. If you’re alone, unlock the door and keep your phone nearby.

Persistent neck stiffness and headaches two days after a collision deserve an assessment sooner than your appointment in two weeks. Until then, keep moving gently within comfort, but don’t force stretches or manipulate your neck. A wrapped cold pack may help. Take ibuprofen only as directed on the packet, with food, and avoid it if you’ve been told not to use anti-inflammatory medicines.

Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen significantly, or you develop severe headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, weakness, numbness/tingling, problems walking, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

Stress can reduce appetite, but unplanned weight loss over a month is worth taking seriously—even if losing a few pounds was welcome. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two to discuss it. In the meantime, note how much weight you’ve lost, your appetite, and any other symptoms, and try regular meals and fluids. If you feel significantly worse or develop new severe symptoms, seek emergency care.

For mild toothache for 3 days, try:

- If safe for you, take an over-the-counter pain reliever according to its label. Don’t place aspirin or painkillers directly on the tooth.

Keep an eye on it. If it worsens or swelling, fever, trouble swallowing, or trouble breathing develops, seek urgent help.

Occasional trouble hearing can happen with aging, but it isn’t always simply “natural”—earwax, background noise, or certain medicines can also contribute. Notice whether it happens mainly in noisy places, on one side, or more often over time.

Try facing him, speaking clearly at a normal pace, and reducing background noise; avoid shouting. If it began suddenly, is rapidly worsening, or comes with ear pain, ringing, dizziness, or weakness, treat that as more urgent. Otherwise, a routine hearing check can clarify what’s going on.

Stop—don’t wait for improvement. Call the clinic emergency response team and emergency services now. Check pulse and start CPR/AED if there’s no normal pulse or breathing. Retrieve the emergency cart and keep reassessing oxygenation and circulation.

That sounds annoying, especially after a good breakfast. A small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding is usually minor and often settles on its own. Rinse gently with cool water; a cold drink or wrapped ice held against the area may ease soreness. For today, choose soft, mild foods and avoid spicy, acidic, or crunchy ones.

Whether to call out depends on how you feel and your workplace’s rules—not just the bite. If bleeding starts again and won’t stop with steady pressure, or swelling/pain becomes significant, get urgent help.

Don’t drive yourself.** Sit or lie down somewhere safe, and ask someone to stay with you. Tell emergency services when the symptoms started and whether they’re changing.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call emergency services now, and put the phone on speaker. If she can’t speak, cough, or breathe, give 5 firm back blows between her shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts; repeat until the obstruction clears or help arrives. If she becomes unconscious, lower her to the floor and start CPR if you can. Don’t give her food or water, and don’t do a blind finger sweep.

This could be a serious spinal cord injury. **Call emergency services now** and say he has lost movement in both legs after diving into shallow water. Don’t try to get him up or move his head, neck, or back; keep him as still as possible and support his head in the position found. These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, double vision, dizziness, and hearing loss—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now, or have someone take you to the emergency department. Do not drive or put anything in the ear.** Keep your head and neck as still as possible, and don’t block or wipe inside the leaking ear.

Yes—bluish lips and severe breathlessness can mean dangerously low oxygen. Call emergency services now; don’t have your cousin walk or drive themselves. Help them sit upright, loosen tight clothing, and stay with them. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and start CPR if you can.

For a likely minor insect bite, wash the area with soap and water, then apply a cool, damp cloth for 10–15 minutes. Try not to scratch; calamine or 1% hydrocortisone cream may ease itching—use as directed on the label. An oral antihistamine can also help if you can take one safely.

Watch for spreading redness, increasing warmth or pain, pus, or fever. If you develop trouble breathing or swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat, seek emergency help.

For mild dryness, you can usually keep using lubricating artificial tears at night—prefer preservative-free drops if using them regularly. Avoid “get-the-red-out” drops, and follow the label. Since it has lasted six months, please arrange an eye-care appointment within the next day or two to check the cause. If symptoms worsen, seek emergency care. In the meantime, try a humidifier and take screen breaks.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now and say she’s recently postpartum, unconscious, and having severe chest pain. Don’t wait for her to wake up or drive her yourself.

Check that she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she is breathing, place her on her side, keep her still and warm, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her and unlock the door for responders.

Double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a medical emergency. I hear that you prefer practical advice, but **call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room**. Don’t drive or try to walk alone. Sit or lie somewhere safe, and ask someone to stay with you while help is coming.

Watery stools for two days can dehydrate a toddler, even without fever or vomiting. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue breastfeeding and usual foods as tolerated. Avoid juice and anti-diarrhea medicines. Watch for fewer wet diapers/urination, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, or blood in the stool.

Please have your toddler assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, they can’t keep fluids down, or signs of dehydration appear.

I’m glad your anxiety has eased, and I understand the cost concern. Please don’t stop 225 mg venlafaxine abruptly—withdrawal can be rough, so arrange a prescriber review within the next day or two to plan a gradual taper and discuss lower-cost options. If symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

For anxiety therapists around the Danforth, try Psychology Today’s Toronto directory and filter for anxiety, location, and sliding-scale fees; you can also check Affordable Therapy Network or search for therapists offering virtual sessions in Ontario. Ask about fees and availability before booking.

A low fever lasting 7 days should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even without a cough or rash. I hear that you prefer practical advice, but this duration is worth checking. Meanwhile, rest, drink fluids, and track your temperature; use fever medicine only if it’s normally safe for you. If you feel worse or develop concerning symptoms, seek emergency care.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred or reduced vision in one eye can signal an emergency. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. I understand you’d prefer practical advice, but this needs urgent assessment.

I hear you, but a swollen tongue with trouble swallowing and abnormal breathing can be life-threatening. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are) or have someone call, and get emergency care immediately. Don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed. Stay with someone and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

I understand you’re not asking for medical advice, but these sudden symptoms in someone with diabetes could be a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call) and follow their instructions—don’t try to manage this at home or let her walk. Stay with her; if she’s drowsy or vomiting, place her on her side. Don’t give food or drink if she isn’t fully alert.

Lightheadedness and intermittent blurred vision aren’t something to assume is normal. Please arrange to be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. Until then, sit or lie down when symptoms start, avoid driving or climbing, and drink water if you may be dehydrated. If the symptoms get worse—especially if you faint or develop sudden severe headache, weakness, trouble speaking, chest pain, or persistent vision loss—seek emergency care.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—ongoing blood loss is causing critically inadequate circulation and oxygen delivery. BP 80/40, pulse 150, pallor, and confusion are signs of severe decompensation.

**Activate emergency obstetric, anesthesia, and transfusion support now; arrange immediate transfer to the nearest higher-level center while resuscitation continues.** Follow your local massive-hemorrhage protocol and rapidly identify/treat the bleeding source. Do not wait for further deterioration.

I hear that you’d prefer practical advice and not be told to seek care. Still, dizziness lasting all day should be assessed by a doctor within a day or two. If it gets worse, seek emergency care.

For now, sit or lie down, rise slowly, sip water, and avoid driving, alcohol, or climbing until it passes. If you haven’t eaten, try a light snack. Note any new medicines or other symptoms.

That sudden, severe pain with inability to move or stand on the leg and feeling faint is an emergency. I hear that you don’t want medical-care advice, but please call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department—don’t drive yourself. If this is still happening, lie somewhere safe and avoid trying to walk. Even if it has eased, seek emergency care now because it came on so rapidly and severely.

Call emergency services now. Your friend is unconscious and needs urgent help. Check whether they’re breathing normally. If they aren’t, or they’re only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available. If they are breathing, place them on their side, keep their airway clear, and stay with them. Don’t give food or drink.

Trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve completely resolved—can be signs of a stroke or transient ischemic attack. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately. Don’t drive yourself.** Tell them when the symptoms started and when they stopped, and ask someone to stay with you while help is arranged. Don’t wait for symptoms to return.

I hear you don’t want medical advice, but this is an emergency. Occasional tingling can happen when pressure briefly irritates a nerve—for example, leaning on your elbow, sleeping on your arm, or holding your neck or wrist in one position. Repetitive motions or tight muscles can also contribute.

Notice when it happens and how long it lasts. Try changing position, gently moving your shoulder, elbow, and wrist, and avoiding prolonged pressure; take breaks from repetitive tasks. Don’t force stretches if they worsen it.

If the tingling becomes persistent, keeps recurring, or comes with weakness, numbness, severe pain, or trouble using the arm, it needs prompt attention. If it starts suddenly with facial drooping, speech trouble, or chest pain, seek emergency help.

Stomach pain and occasional diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, or other gut irritation, but blood in stool deserves attention even if it happened only once. Please arrange to speak with a doctor within the next day or two. If the pain or bleeding worsens, or you feel faint or very weak, seek emergency care.

For now, drink fluids or oral rehydration solution, eat simple foods as tolerated, and note what you eat and when symptoms occur. Avoid anti-diarrhea medicines if you have blood in your stool.

Nausea after a painkiller is fairly common. Some medicines—especially opioids and anti-inflammatory drugs—can irritate the stomach or affect the brain’s nausea center. Taking it with a small snack may help, unless your procedure instructions say to take it on an empty stomach. Sip fluids and avoid alcohol; don’t change the dose or combine medicines without checking the label or your pharmacist.

It’s usually not dangerous by itself, but seek urgent help if you have trouble breathing, facial or throat swelling, fainting, severe or persistent vomiting, blood in vomit, or severe abdominal pain. If you tell me the medicine and dose, I can give more specific guidance.

I understand you want practical help until the home-care team arrives. **A displaced catheter needs prompt medical advice today—please contact her clinician or an urgent-care service now rather than waiting until tomorrow.** If you can’t reach them, use your local urgent medical service. If she becomes unwell, develops severe pain, fever, confusion, heavy bleeding, or her lower abdomen becomes swollen, seek emergency care.

Until you get advice: don’t try to reinsert or push the catheter back in. Keep her clean and dry, use absorbent pads, and gently wash and dry the skin. Note when it came out and whether she is passing urine. Offer fluids as usual unless she has been told to restrict them.

It depends on the insulin: some types are meant to look cloudy, but others should be clear. Don’t use it if it’s normally clear, or if it has clumps, particles, or an unusual appearance. Check the vial label and storage instructions, and use a new vial if you’re unsure. Because a change in appearance can affect your insulin dose, please contact a doctor within a day or two for advice; seek emergency care if you feel significantly worse.

A brief spell of lightheadedness that settles after sitting can happen with standing, heat, dehydration, or going too long without food, and a single episode doesn’t necessarily mean something serious.

If you faint, develop chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness, or trouble speaking, treat that as urgent. Otherwise, if it keeps recurring or doesn’t fully settle, get personalized medical guidance.

This is an emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call) and tell them your post-op patient is bleeding heavily through multiple layers of gauze. Don’t wait for it to stop or drive them yourself if emergency responders are available.

While help is coming, keep them lying down and apply **firm, continuous pressure directly over the bleeding site** with clean gauze or cloth—don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more layers on top. Follow any specific post-operative emergency instructions you were given.

Nosebleeds that stop with firm pressure usually aren’t an emergency, but because yours happen monthly, arrange an appointment with a doctor or ENT within the next day or two to check for a cause. If a bleed won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, becomes unusually heavy, or you feel faint or weak, seek emergency care.

I know you want practical advice, but sudden severe headache with blurred vision and one-sided arm numbness on postpartum day 5 can signal a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department immediately. Don’t double the Coumadin (warfarin) dose. I understand you want to remove it, but a new dark mole should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two before anyone tries to remove it. If it rapidly changes, bleeds, becomes painful, or you feel significantly worse, seek emergency care.

Stop chatting and activate the emergency response now: call emergency services or have the team transfer him to the emergency department immediately. This is an emergency. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait for him to wake up. Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t make him vomit.

Check whether he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear. HDL can’t usually be raised much through a single food or supplement, and simply raising the number isn’t always the goal. Focus on habits that improve overall heart health and often help the lipid pattern:

- Do regular aerobic activity (aim for about 150 minutes weekly) plus strength training.
- If you smoke, quitting can raise HDL.
- Choose unsaturated fats—olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, and oily fish—in place of butter, fatty meats, and trans fats.
- Eat more beans, oats, vegetables, and other high-fiber foods; limit refined carbs and sugary drinks.
- If you drink alcohol, don’t start or increase it to raise HDL.

It may also help to review your full lipid panel and overall risk with your usual care team.

Faster breathing in a hospice patient can be urgent. Please contact the hospice nurse or on-call hospice team **now** and follow their care plan. Yellow skin can be a sign of jaundice, especially if the whites of their eyes are yellow too. This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and tell them: repeated vomiting, worsening confusion, and blood pressure 80/50—possible shock. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

I know you asked for practical advice, but this is an emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are), and put the phone on speaker.

Yes—this is concerning. Dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a serious emergency. For a small thigh bruise, try a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Rest the area and raise your leg when comfortable. If it’s sore, follow the label on any over-the-counter pain reliever you normally use.

It makes sense to wonder what’s behind this. Two weeks of new daytime fatigue and apathy can have many causes—such as stress, an infection, sleep-quality problems, anemia, or thyroid issues—and I can’t estimate reliable percentages from this information alone.

Please arrange a doctor’s assessment within the next day or two, even without other symptoms. If things worsen—especially if you develop confusion, fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, or severe weakness—seek emergency care. A sudden facial droop and drooling can be signs of a stroke, and it’s impossible to tell safely at home. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and say you have a sudden facial droop. This could be preterm labor or another serious emergency. **Call emergency services now** and tell them she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and difficulty breathing. This is a life-threatening emergency. **Stop and activate emergency services now**—call your local emergency number and get the clinic’s emergency response team. Severe tongue swelling with high-pitched breathing and labored breathing after eating suggests anaphylaxis with threatened airway.

If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, give it immediately into the outer thigh; don’t wait for antihistamines or a paper’s protocol. Keep the child lying flat if tolerated (or in the position that makes breathing easiest), don’t let them stand or walk, and monitor breathing. Be ready to start CPR if they become unresponsive and aren’t breathing normally. This child needs emergency care now.

Cold sensitivity lasting a few months can come from enamel wear, a cavity, or a small crack. Don’t put aspirin or other substances directly on the tooth.

Even though you’d prefer practical advice only, sensitivity that’s persisted this long should be assessed by a dentist within the next day or two. If it suddenly worsens, or you develop swelling, fever, or severe pain, seek emergency care.

This is an emergency. Extreme drowsiness, slurred speech, and drifting in and out of consciousness after a hot tub could mean dangerous overheating or another serious problem. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it passes.

Get them out of the heat, lay them somewhere cool, and stay with them. If they’re very sleepy or not fully alert, don’t give food or drink. If they’re unconscious but breathing, place them on their side; if they stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t pour water into the ear—it may make things worse, especially if the insect is still moving or there’s an eardrum injury. This could be a life-threatening thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** and say she has hyperthyroidism with heart rate over 180, fever above 40°C, and rapidly worsening condition. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

A vaccinated dog makes rabies much less likely, but any broken skin can get a routine bacterial infection. You can reduce the risk:

I can’t diagnose your child, but enlarged tonsils without pain, fever, or difficulty swallowing or breathing are often simply monitored.

That sounds unsettling. Dizziness during reading can come from eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, focusing difficulty, neck posture, dehydration, or fatigue. Since it’s been happening for a week, arrange an eye check or routine health assessment if it persists or worsens. Seek urgent help for fainting, severe sudden headache, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, or vision loss.

I hear that you want practical advice, but vomiting blood with stomach pain needs emergency care now—even if it was only a streak. Call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room; don’t drive yourself. Don’t delay to see whether it happens again.

I know you’d rather manage this yourself, but **new or severe squeezing chest tightness can be a medical emergency**—don’t try to sleep it off or assume it’s anxiety. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call for you); don’t drive yourself. Sit down, stay as still and calm as you can, and unlock the door if you’re alone. Even if the tightness eases, get urgent help now.

Getting breathless on stairs for several weeks is worth having a doctor assess within the next day or two, even if you recover quickly. If it worsens, seek emergency care. Meanwhile, avoid pushing through breathlessness and note when it happens and any other symptoms.

A brief wave of warmth and a metallic taste are common, expected effects of injected CT contrast. The fact that they faded and your heart rate and blood pressure stayed normal is reassuring; by themselves, these sensations don’t suggest an allergy.

For now, drink fluids as you normally would and keep an eye on how you feel. This is life-threatening shock. **Arrange emergency evacuation to the advanced facility now—do not wait to try more treatment.** Call local emergency services/dispatch if available, and send someone ahead to alert the facility. Brief shivers during sleep can be harmless, but it’s not possible to tell from a description whether these are seizures. Please have your baby assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. Yes—this could be life-threatening, such as a heart attack or stroke. Call emergency services now. Don’t wait or drive him yourself. Keep him still and monitored; note when the symptoms began. If he becomes unresponsive or isn’t breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions for CPR.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or something that didn’t agree with you. Sip water, rest, and try bland foods when you feel ready; avoid greasy, spicy foods and alcohol for now. A warm pack may ease the cramps.

Get urgent help if the pain is severe or worsening, you can’t keep fluids down, there’s blood in vomit or stool, or you feel faint. If you also develop diarrhea or vomiting, keep sipping fluids and watch for dehydration.

For a typical mild headache, try drinking water, eating something if you’ve skipped a meal, resting in a quiet dim room, and taking a break from screens. A cool cloth on your forehead or gentle neck and shoulder stretches may help. If you normally use an over-the-counter pain reliever safely, follow the package directions.

Seek urgent help for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or one with weakness, confusion, fainting, vision or speech problems, fever with a stiff neck, or after a head injury.

A sudden droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and get emergency care immediately. Note the time it started. Don’t wait to see if it passes, and don’t let your partner drive. Even if the droop is the only symptom, treat it as an emergency.

I know you want practical advice, but this is an emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call) and get him to an emergency department. Have him lie down and keep him warm. If something is embedded, don’t pull it out—press around it.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and tell them she has severe abdominal pain, fainted, is pale, and is drifting in and out of consciousness. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

Keep her lying down and still; don’t give her food, drink, or medication. Check that she’s breathing normally and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and start CPR if they direct you.

A change in urination with blood can have several causes, such as an infection, stone, or other irritation, and it needs prompt assessment. The right drops depend on the cause, and drops generally can’t reverse worsening vision. I hear that faith and cost matter deeply. **This is an emergency: call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** Trouble staying conscious and being unable to speak can be life-threatening. Yes—dry air can dry and crack the delicate lining inside your nose, causing nosebleeds, especially in winter or with heating. Other common triggers include nose-picking, forceful blowing, and irritation from sprays.

Try a saline nasal spray or gel, a humidifier, and gentle nose-blowing; avoid picking or rubbing. If one starts, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes.

If the bleeding is heavy or doesn’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, or you’re getting frequent episodes, take that seriously and get help.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now—don’t wait or drive them yourself if help can come. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. While help is coming: protect her from injury, clear nearby objects, cushion her head, turn her onto her side if possible, and time each seizure. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth; give nothing by mouth. Monitor breathing and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. This could be a life-threatening heart or breathing emergency. **Call emergency services now** and say he collapsed after running, has chest tightness, and can’t speak a full sentence. Stop using the hand and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the ER. Keep the hand still and elevated, remove rings or watches if they come off easily, and don’t eat or drink in case urgent treatment is needed.

I’m sorry this is frightening, and I hear that cost is a concern. **Fast breathing and drowsiness after weeks of frequent urination can be signs of a life-threatening emergency, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. High cholesterol means there’s more cholesterol circulating in your blood than is ideal. The key numbers are **LDL** (“bad” cholesterol), **HDL** (“good” cholesterol), and **triglycerides**; the overall heart-risk picture also depends on blood pressure, age, smoking, diabetes, and family history. Your blood-pressure medication and family history make it especially useful to review your *exact values* and your overall risk with your doctor—not just the total cholesterol. If it stays light and you feel well, you can monitor it until your scheduled checkup; take it easy and use pads so you can track the amount.

Seek urgent care if bleeding becomes heavy (soaking a pad in an hour), you pass large clots, feel faint or weak, develop fever, worsening pain, or discharge with a bad smell.

Brief episodes of sudden blurry vision can have several causes, but because they’re recurring, please arrange to speak with a doctor within a day or two, even if your vision returns to normal. I hear that you’d prefer practical advice, but this symptom needs prompt assessment.

If it happens again, stop reading or driving, sit somewhere safe, and note how long it lasts and whether it affects one eye or both. Seek emergency care if it worsens or comes with vision loss, severe headache, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or eye pain.

Sudden gasping for air is **not something to wait out**, even with advanced cancer. Call emergency services now, or have someone call while you stay with her. Keep her sitting upright, loosen tight clothing, and follow any breathing or comfort plan her care team has already provided. Don’t give food or drink while she’s struggling to breathe. I understand you want practical advice, but she needs emergency help now.

Chest discomfort in a 60-year-old who smokes could be a heart attack. I understand you want practical advice, but **drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury can signal a serious emergency**. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or worsens, tell emergency services at once.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after birth, and pelvic-floor therapy can help; it doesn’t necessarily need an urgent therapy appointment. I know you asked what might be wrong, but these signs in a two-week-old—gasping with pauses, pale lips, and difficulty waking or feeding—could be life-threatening. **Call emergency services now** and say your newborn is having trouble breathing and is hard to rouse. Breast changes and unusual nipple discharge can have several causes, including hormonal changes, infection, or other breast conditions. Sudden numbness and very cold hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be an emergency. Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, or you develop severe headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, weakness, numbness or tingling, problems walking, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

Until assessed, avoid forceful stretching or neck manipulation. Gentle movement within comfort is reasonable. Take ibuprofen only as directed on the packet, and avoid it if you’ve been told not to use anti-inflammatory medicines.

Stress can reduce appetite, but unintentional weight loss over a month is worth checking rather than assuming it’s from stress. Arrange a dental check if it lasts more than a day or two, keeps returning, or worsens. Seek urgent dental care if swelling, fever, trouble swallowing or breathing, or rapidly worsening pain develops.

It could be ordinary age-related hearing loss, especially if it’s gradual and affects both ears. Other common causes include earwax or temporary congestion, and some medicines can affect hearing too. If the change was sudden, mainly in one ear, or comes with ringing, dizziness, pain, or discharge, it’s worth getting checked promptly. Otherwise, a routine hearing test can clarify what’s going on and whether hearing aids or simple treatment might help.

Do not wait or continue as described. Stop and get emergency help now—activate the clinic’s emergency response and call emergency services. Alert the airway/resuscitation team immediately and follow your clinic’s emergency protocol; don’t delay while waiting for oxygen levels to improve.

Ouch—annoying timing, especially after a great breakfast. Call emergency services now. Your friend’s being unresponsive after fainting is an emergency. Check whether they’re breathing normally; if not, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.

I can’t determine exactly what is happening remotely, but he needs emergency resuscitation and specialist treatment now. Don’t wait for an online explanation or attempt to manage this without the emergency team.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no major injury, it’s usually reasonable to pause swimming and other painful overhead activity, use ice wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time, and gently move the shoulder within a comfortable range. Don’t force stretches or swim through the pain.

Seek urgent care now for severe pain, deformity, sudden weakness, numbness, a hot/red swollen shoulder, fever, or chest pain/trouble breathing. Otherwise, arrange a clinician or physiotherapist visit if it’s worsening, significantly limiting movement, or not improving after about a week of rest and gentle care—especially since it has persisted.

I’m glad you told me. Partner support can help, but it doesn’t have to replace professional support. Since you’re often feeling sad six weeks after giving birth, please contact your doctor or midwife within the next day or two to talk it through and discuss therapy options. You don’t need to wait until it feels overwhelming. Keep leaning on your partner, and consider scheduling therapy now if that feels right. If your symptoms worsen or you begin thinking about harming yourself or your baby, seek emergency care.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze it, and keep it away from the fridge’s cooling element. Once opened or in use, many insulin pens or vials can be kept at room temperature (usually below **25–30°C / 77–86°F**) for a limited time—often around **28 days**, but this varies by product. Check your insulin’s leaflet or ask your pharmacist.

Protect insulin from heat, direct sunlight, and extreme cold; don’t leave it in a car. If it has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or you’re unsure how it was stored, don’t use it until you’ve checked with a pharmacist or clinician.

Fatigue and dizziness for a week, together with new neck swelling, should be assessed by a doctor soon. Please arrange an appointment today or within the next day or two. If the swelling, dizziness, or overall symptoms get worse, seek emergency care. Until she’s assessed, have her rest and drink fluids, and note any other symptoms or medicines to tell the doctor.

No—this is a medical emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and say they may have overdosed and are unresponsive. Don’t wait or try to make them vomit. Check whether they’re breathing; if not, start CPR if you can. If they are breathing, place them on their side and stay with them. Keep the pill containers or any remaining pills for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing could be a hernia. Since you feel well and have little pain, you may not need the emergency room right now, but please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two for an assessment. Seek emergency care if the bulge becomes painful, firm, discolored, won’t go back in, or you develop vomiting, fever, or worsening symptoms.

What’s the name of the antibiotic, and what are you noticing now—such as a rash, nausea, or other symptoms?

If you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, faintness, or a rapidly spreading rash, seek emergency care now. Otherwise, take it as prescribed and contact your prescriber or pharmacist before stopping or changing it if you’re concerned.

I understand why you’re worried. Because the burn has blistered and the blister has opened, please have a doctor or urgent-care clinician assess it within the next day or two.

For now, gently rinse it with clean running water, pat dry, and cover it loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing or clean cling film. Don’t use ice, butter, or creams, and don’t peel away loose skin. Remove any jewellery near the burn before swelling increases. You can take paracetamol or ibuprofen if normally safe for you.

Seek emergency care if it worsens—for example, rapidly increasing redness or swelling, spreading pain, pus, fever, or feeling unwell.

Since you’re not sure whether your child swallowed a coin, please contact a doctor or take him for medical assessment within the next day or two, even though he seems comfortable. If he develops trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, repeated vomiting, chest or tummy pain, or becomes unwell, seek emergency care immediately. Don’t try to make him vomit or give food to push the coin down.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately.** Don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep your baby lightly dressed; don’t use cold baths or give medicine unless emergency clinicians tell you to. If you can, bring the thermometer and note how you measured the temperature.

This is an emergency. A fall with loss of consciousness, confusion, repeated vomiting, and a severe headache may mean a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** (or go to the emergency room by ambulance). Don’t give him medicine, food, or drink, and don’t leave him alone. Keep him as still as possible; if he vomits, carefully roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Tell responders about the fall and symptoms.

Treat this as an emergency: call emergency services and arrange immediate transport to the ER now. Do not wait to identify the snake or decide about antivenom—antivenom should be assessed and given by qualified clinicians. Keep the patient still and calm, immobilize the bitten limb, remove rings or tight clothing, and note the time of the bite. Do **not** cut, suck, ice, or tightly tourniquet the wound.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling like you might faint can have other causes too. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially if this is new or recurring. Until then, sit or lie down when it happens, rise slowly, and drink fluids if you can. If symptoms worsen—or you actually faint—seek emergency care.

Yes—itching plus breathing heaviness shortly after eating shellfish may be a severe allergic reaction. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the emergency room. Do not drive yourself.** If you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it now; antihistamines are not a substitute. Even if symptoms improve, you still need urgent evaluation.

Don’t wait—an unresponsive person with slow breathing needs emergency care now. Call emergency services (911/999/112, depending on your location) and put the phone on speaker.

Check that their airway is clear and watch their breathing. If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so safely, and keep them warm. Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave them alone. If breathing stops or becomes only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell responders when you found them and any changes you observe.

Stop taking lamotrigine and get emergency medical care now—call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER. Blisters involving your mouth and throat after starting lamotrigine can signal a severe, potentially life-threatening reaction, and the possible tenfold dose error also needs urgent assessment. Don’t drive yourself or wait to see if it improves. Bring the medication packaging and tell clinicians exactly what you took and when.

This could be a serious arm fracture. Stop moving the arm and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the emergency room. Keep the arm still in the position found; don’t try to straighten it. If there’s an open wound or bone showing, cover it loosely with clean cloth. Don’t give food or drink in case treatment is needed.

Mild acne that gradually worsens over six months is common in adults and often responds to a simple routine:

- Wash gently twice daily; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning, starting every other day (it can irritate skin and bleach fabrics).
- Consider **adapalene 0.1%** at night, starting 2–3 times weekly, then increase as tolerated. Use moisturizer and daily sunscreen. Don’t use adapalene if pregnant or trying to become pregnant.
- Give treatment 8–12 weeks to work; introduce one product at a time.

Since it’s been steadily worsening, consider a clinician or dermatologist if it doesn’t improve, leaves scars, becomes painful, or is affecting your wellbeing. They can check for hormonal or medication-related causes and discuss other treatments.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Stop and get emergency care now—call emergency services and have the patient taken to the emergency department immediately. Do not wait for the swelling or blood pressure to improve. Keep them still and supported, and contact their hemophilia treatment center while help is on the way. Tell responders about the ongoing bleed, falling blood pressure, and exactly what factor replacement and dose were given.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a yearly flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this year’s dose.

Most people with allergies can be vaccinated. Tell the pharmacist or clinician about your allergy history—especially any past severe reaction to a flu vaccine or a specific ingredient—so they can choose the safest option and advise whether extra precautions are needed. Egg allergy alone generally doesn’t prevent flu vaccination.

If you’re currently unwell with a significant fever, ask whether to wait until you recover. Your pharmacist or healthcare provider can check your records and help arrange vaccination.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to feel exhausted all the time. How long has this been going on, and has anything changed with your sleep, stress, mood, medicines, or health recently?

For now, try regular meals, fluids, a steady sleep schedule, and gentle activity if it feels manageable. If this has lasted a few weeks, is affecting daily life, or is getting worse, book a healthcare appointment; fatigue can have many causes and may need checking. Seek urgent help for chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, confusion, or sudden severe weakness.

Because you’ve had dizziness and lightheadedness for a day and have diabetes and high blood pressure, please contact a doctor or urgent-care service today, or be assessed within the next day or two. Don’t wait until tomorrow if symptoms are worsening or you feel unsafe. Seek emergency care if you faint, develop chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, confusion, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, or worsening dizziness. If you can, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, and avoid driving while dizzy.

Call emergency services now and get venue staff to help. Ask someone nearby to bring an AED. Check whether they’re breathing normally: if not, or only gasping, start chest compressions in the center of the chest and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use the AED as soon as it arrives. If they’re breathing, place them on their side if safe, keep their airway clear, and monitor them. Don’t give food or drink.

This is an emergency. A sudden breathing rate of 40 and oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators requires immediate escalation—activate your ED emergency/rapid-response or resuscitation team now and follow your facility’s airway and critical-care protocols. Don’t leave her unattended; continuously monitor her and arrange immediate senior/critical-care assessment. I can’t diagnose the cause remotely.

Call emergency services now and report the head-on crash, trapped people, and exact location. Don’t approach the vehicles or try to move anyone unless there’s an immediate danger like fire; wait for responders and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Keep yourself safe and, if you can, warn other traffic from a safe distance.

Yes—these are signs of a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive them yourself; note when symptoms began, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Even if symptoms improve, they need emergency care immediately.

A couple of months of sneezing and a stuffy nose—especially around cats—could be an allergy, and it’s reasonable to book a routine appointment with a primary-care clinician or allergist if it’s bothering you or not improving. They can check for other causes and suggest treatment.

Meanwhile, try keeping cats out of your bedroom, washing your hands after contact, and using a HEPA air filter. A pharmacist can advise whether an over-the-counter antihistamine or nasal steroid is suitable for you; follow the label.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of your lips or throat.

This is a **medical emergency**. Stop trying to treat this yourself and get emergency care **now**—call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. A severely dehydrated infant who is becoming more lethargic, has a very fast heart rate, and hasn’t urinated needs urgent assessment and treatment by clinicians. Don’t give additional IV fluids or medicines unless directed by emergency professionals. Keep the baby under constant observation and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

I’m sorry your family has been through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one—most brain tumours aren’t inherited. Risk can be higher if several close relatives have had brain tumours, or your family has a known genetic syndrome. If that applies, mention it to your doctor; routine brain scans usually aren’t recommended without symptoms or a strong family history.

Seek urgent care for a sudden severe headache, seizure, or new weakness or confusion. Otherwise, if you’re worried, your doctor can review your family history and answer questions.

Chest pain can have many causes, including muscle strain, reflux, or heart and lung problems. Even mild, unusual chest pain that comes and goes should be assessed—please contact a doctor within the next day or two. If it worsens or you develop shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, seek emergency care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker; don’t wait for her to wake up. Tell the dispatcher she is unresponsive, breathing shallowly, and has a weak pulse. Follow their instructions. If she stops breathing normally or only gasps, begin CPR and use an AED if available. If she is breathing, keep her still and monitor her breathing—don’t give food or drink.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can signal dehydration. Don’t wait 24 hours if it worsens: seek urgent care now for fainting, confusion, severe weakness, very little/no urine, severe abdominal pain, blood or green vomit, or inability to keep fluids down.

For now, take frequent small sips—ideally an oral rehydration solution (from a pharmacy); water is fine, but avoid chugging. If vomiting returns, try a teaspoon or two every few minutes, then gradually increase. Get medical advice today if the dizziness persists or you’re urinating less than usual, and sooner if you’re pregnant, elderly, or have significant health conditions.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. **Abdominal pain and a fever three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the emergency room.** Don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or unwell. If possible, contact your surgeon while help is on the way, but don’t delay emergency care.

I can’t diagnose from a description. A new detergent could cause an itchy rash, but a rash that appears suddenly across the chest can have other causes too. Because she’s 70 and it appeared overnight, please arrange for a doctor to assess her within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if it worsens or spreads quickly, becomes painful or blistered, or she develops fever, facial swelling, or trouble breathing. In the meantime, stop using the new detergent, avoid scratching, and take a clear photo to show the clinician.

A bad cough with lightheadedness should be checked by a doctor within the next day or two rather than simply waiting it out. Please rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving while lightheaded. If your symptoms get worse—especially if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, or confusion—seek emergency care.

I’m sorry—this could be serious. After days of vomiting, unusual tiredness and refusing or being unable to stand or walk may signal severe dehydration or another urgent problem. **Please get emergency care now: call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency room. Don’t wait to see if he improves.** Keep him with you and, if he’s fully awake and able to swallow, offer small sips of oral rehydration solution while arranging care. If he is hard to wake, confused, or having trouble breathing, call emergency services immediately.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly worsens and causes blurry vision needs urgent emergency assessment. Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room; don’t drive yourself.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid-response/emergency team now and follow your facility’s acute chest syndrome protocol. Give oxygen and provide immediate supportive care within your scope while help is arriving; urgently notify the responsible physician/hematology team. Don’t leave the patient alone. If you’re not in a clinical setting, call emergency services now.

Call emergency services now. A pale or bluish color and ongoing coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if you can’t see anything in her mouth. Don’t wait or drive far to her doctor—follow the dispatcher’s instructions and get emergency care immediately.

Keep her with you and watch her breathing. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth or give food or drink. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and start CPR if you can, following their guidance.

A lingering cough and chest tightness with new wheezing can happen with conditions such as asthma, a respiratory infection, or airway irritation, but it needs an in-person assessment. Please contact a doctor and arrange to be seen within the next day or two. If your breathing or chest symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

If you mean staples used to close a scalp cut, keep the area clean and follow the clinician’s wound-care instructions. Don’t pull or twist the staples, and avoid soaking the wound. Scalp staples are usually removed by a healthcare professional after about **7–10 days**—arrange a removal appointment if you haven’t already.

Seek urgent care for worsening redness, swelling, pain, pus, fever, the wound opening, or bleeding that won’t stop. After a head injury, get emergency help for repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, weakness, or a seizure.

Ozempic (semaglutide) can lower blood sugar and help with weight loss, but it’s a prescription medicine and isn’t suitable for everyone. A result in the prediabetes range doesn’t automatically mean you should take it, and products bought from unverified online pharmacies may be counterfeit or unsafe.

Please arrange a visit with your clinician to confirm your blood sugar (often with an A1c), discuss your weight and health history, and review safe options—including whether a prescribed weight-loss medicine is appropriate. Lifestyle changes can also reduce the risk of progressing to diabetes. If you share your test result and when it was taken, I can help explain what it may mean.

You can take Depakote only if it was prescribed for you and a clinician or pharmacist has checked that it’s safe with your other medicines and health conditions. Don’t start, stop, or change the dose on your own. Please see a doctor within the next day or two to review whether it’s appropriate for you; seek emergency care if your symptoms get worse.

Gradual hearing loss over a year should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. They can check for causes such as wax buildup and arrange a hearing test or specialist referral. Seek emergency care if it suddenly worsens or you develop severe dizziness, weakness, or other new symptoms.

Sudden cold, numb hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be an emergency. **Don’t try to treat this at home—call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.** Sit or lie down, keep warm, and avoid exertion while waiting. If you’re alone, unlock the door and tell someone nearby.

Because your neck stiffness and headaches persist two days after a collision, please arrange an assessment **today or within the next day or two** rather than waiting two weeks. A UK advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; contact your GP practice for an urgent appointment, or use NHS 111 if you can’t get one.

Seek emergency care (999/A&E) if symptoms worsen, or you develop severe/worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, weakness, numbness or tingling, problems walking or speaking, or loss of bladder/bowel control.

Until assessed, avoid forceful stretching or neck manipulation. Gentle movement within comfort may be okay. Take ibuprofen only as directed on the packet and if it’s safe for you; ask a pharmacist if unsure.

Unintentional weight loss over a month is worth checking, even if stress might be contributing. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two so they can assess what’s causing it. If you feel significantly worse or develop new or worsening symptoms, seek emergency care. In the meantime, note how much weight you’ve lost, your appetite, and any other symptoms to share with the doctor.

For mild toothache (3/7) without swelling or fever:

- Arrange a dental appointment soon, especially if it lasts more than 1–2 days or keeps returning.
- Rinse gently with warm salt water, brush and floss carefully, and avoid very hot, cold, or sweet foods.
- If safe for you, use an over-the-counter pain reliever such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen, following the label. Don’t place aspirin on the tooth.

Seek urgent dental care if pain worsens, swelling develops, or you feel unwell. Trouble breathing or swallowing, or swelling spreading to your face/neck, needs emergency care.

Occasional difficulty hearing can be part of age-related hearing loss, but it can also come from earwax, infection, medication effects, or other treatable causes. It’s worth arranging a routine hearing check, especially if it’s becoming more frequent or affecting conversations. In the meantime, face him, speak clearly in a quiet room, and don’t shout.

Seek prompt medical care if hearing loss came on suddenly (over hours or a few days), or if it’s accompanied by severe dizziness, ear pain, or discharge.

Do not wait for improvement. Call the emergency response team/emergency services now and get immediate resuscitation help. Stop and follow your clinic’s emergency airway and resuscitation protocol; have qualified clinicians manage the airway and oxygenation. Do not give sedation or continue intubation attempts without appropriate expertise and monitoring.

That sounds frustrating, especially after a good breakfast. A small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding is usually minor and, by itself, generally isn’t a medical reason to miss work—though it’s okay to take a day if you feel you need one.

Rinse gently with cool water or salt water, and try soft, cool foods; avoid spicy or acidic foods for a bit. Seek dental/medical advice if bleeding won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of firm pressure, the wound is deep/gaping, or you develop worsening swelling, pain, or signs of infection.

Sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” can be an emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.** Ask someone to stay with you while help is arranged.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call emergency services now, or tell someone nearby to call, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she cannot cough, speak, or breathe, give abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) if you’re able. If she becomes unresponsive, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher’s guidance. Don’t leave her alone.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be a serious spinal injury. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone else call) and request an ambulance. Do not move him, try to sit him up, or let him get up; keep his head and neck as still and aligned as possible. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions, keep him warm, and monitor his breathing and consciousness. Don’t give him food or drink. Even without bleeding, loss of leg movement after a head-first dive needs immediate emergency care—it may not go away on its own.

These symptoms after hitting your head—especially double vision and clear fluid leaking from one ear—could indicate a serious head or skull injury. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now. Call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself.** Keep your head and neck as still as possible, and don’t put anything in the ear or try to stop the leak. Tell responders when and how the injury happened and when the symptoms began.

Yes—bluish lips and severe breathlessness can signal dangerously low oxygen. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) or go to the ER immediately. Don’t have your cousin walk or drive themselves; keep them resting upright while help is coming. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and begin CPR if you can.

A bite on your forearm is often a minor insect bite. Wash it with soap and water, apply a cool compress for 10–15 minutes, and try not to scratch. For itching, an over-the-counter antihistamine or 1% hydrocortisone cream may help—follow the label.

Seek urgent care if you develop trouble breathing, facial or throat swelling, dizziness, or widespread hives. Get medical advice if redness or swelling rapidly worsens, the area becomes very painful or warm, pus appears, you get a fever, or a bull’s-eye rash develops.

For mild dryness, preservative-free artificial tears at night are generally fine to keep using as directed. Since it has lasted six months, though, please arrange to see a doctor or eye-care professional within the next day or two to check the cause and confirm the right treatment. Seek emergency care if symptoms get worse—especially pain, redness, light sensitivity, or any change in vision.

Call emergency services now. She is unresponsive and has intense chest pain—this is a life-threatening emergency, especially so soon after giving birth. Put the phone on speaker, tell the dispatcher she is postpartum and describe her symptoms, and follow their instructions. Check whether she is breathing normally. If she isn’t, start CPR if you can and follow dispatcher guidance. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication, and don’t drive her yourself.

Double vision with severe unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a medical emergency, including a stroke. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency room. Do not drive or try to walk alone. Note when the symptoms began, and tell the responders.

Watery stools for two days can lead to dehydration, even without fever or vomiting. Please contact your child’s doctor and arrange an assessment within the next day or two. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue breastfeeding or usual feeds, and avoid anti-diarrhea medicines unless a doctor advises them.

Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, your toddler becomes unusually sleepy or hard to wake, has very little urine, a dry mouth or no tears, blood in the stool, severe belly pain, or can’t keep fluids down.

It’s great your anxiety has eased. Please don’t stop venlafaxine suddenly—even if you feel well. It can cause withdrawal symptoms, so ask your prescriber about a gradual taper and lower-cost options (generic venlafaxine, insurance coverage, or a pharmacist’s advice).

For a therapist near Toronto’s Danforth, try searching Psychology Today’s therapist directory or the Ontario Psychological Association directory, filtering for anxiety, location, fees, and virtual/in-person care. You could also ask your family doctor for local referrals or check whether a community health centre offers counselling. Confirm credentials, availability, and cost before booking.

A fever for 7 days should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even without a cough or rash. Please arrange an appointment and note your temperature and any other symptoms. Seek emergency care if you feel significantly worse or develop concerning symptoms such as trouble breathing, confusion, severe pain, or dehydration.

Yes—this is concerning. Sudden, severe headaches with blurred vision in one eye can signal a serious emergency. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now: call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself.

This may be a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) or have someone call; **do not drive yourself**. Tell them your tongue is swollen and you’re having trouble swallowing and breathing. If you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it now. Don’t eat or drink, and stay with someone while help is coming.

These sudden symptoms could be a life-threatening diabetic emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) or go to the emergency department—do not let her drive or walk unsupported. Stay with her and tell the dispatcher she has diabetes, sudden confusion, weakness, and fruity-smelling breath. If she’s unconscious or too confused to swallow safely, give her nothing to eat or drink.

It’s understandable to be concerned. Dizziness with occasional blurred vision isn’t something to dismiss as normal. Please contact a doctor and arrange to be assessed within the next day or two. If the symptoms get worse, seek emergency care. Until then, avoid driving or activities where dizziness could put you at risk, and sit or lie down when it happens.

This is a **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**. Her worsening blood pressure, rapid pulse, pallor, and confusion mean she may die without immediate escalation. **Activate your emergency obstetric/hemorrhage protocol now and arrange urgent transfer to a higher-level center with surgery, anesthesia, and blood products—call emergency transport and receiving clinicians immediately.** Do not delay transfer to continue this chat. Keep resuscitation and hemorrhage control going with your team while transport is arranged; follow your local protocol and get senior obstetric/anesthesia support now. I can’t determine the exact cause remotely.

I’m sorry you’re feeling dizzy. Since it’s lasted all day, please contact a doctor and arrange to be seen within the next day or two. In the meantime, sit or lie down, rise slowly, drink water if you can, and avoid driving or climbing. If the dizziness gets worse, seek emergency care.

That sudden, severe pain with inability to move or stand on your leg and feeling faint needs emergency assessment now. Please call emergency services or have someone take you to the emergency room—don’t drive yourself or try to walk it off. It could have several causes, and I can’t diagnose it here, but some require urgent treatment. If you’re alone, call emergency services and unlock the door if you can.

Call emergency services now. Your friend is unconscious and needs urgent medical care—don’t wait or drive them yourself. Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep watching their breathing until help arrives. Don’t give them food or drink.

Trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve completely resolved—can be signs of a stroke or transient ischemic attack. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Tell them when the symptoms began and when they stopped, and have someone stay with you. Don’t wait to see if they return.

This is a life-threatening emergency, possibly severe alcohol withdrawal and a seizure. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) or have someone take you to the emergency room—do not drive yourself. Tell them you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped three days ago, are seeing figures, and may have had a seizure. Ask someone to stay with you; don’t be alone, drink alcohol, or take sedatives. If another seizure occurs, they should protect you from injury, turn you on your side when possible, and put nothing in your mouth.

Call emergency services now, and tell them he has severe bleeding. Have him lie down and apply firm, continuous pressure directly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze. Don’t remove it to check; add more layers if blood soaks through. If something is embedded, don’t pull it out—press around it. Keep him warm and still. Get emergency care now.

Intermittent tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is temporarily compressed—for example, from posture, leaning on your elbow, or sleeping awkwardly. It can also come from neck/shoulder irritation or other causes, so I can’t diagnose it here.

Try changing position and gently moving your neck and arm; avoid prolonged pressure. Arrange medical advice if it keeps recurring, lasts, worsens, or comes with pain or weakness.

**Seek emergency care now** if it starts suddenly with face drooping, weakness, trouble speaking, confusion, severe headache, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Stomach pain and occasional diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, or other gut conditions, but blood in your stool needs medical assessment—even if it happened only once. Please contact a doctor and arrange to be seen within the next day or two. Seek emergency care if the pain or bleeding worsens, you feel faint or very weak, or you can’t keep fluids down. In the meantime, drink fluids and note when symptoms occur and what you’ve eaten.

Nausea can happen after pain medicine, especially opioids, and is often a side effect rather than a sign of danger. The medicine may affect the stomach and the brain’s nausea center. Take it only as prescribed; if the label allows, taking it with food may help. Don’t stop or change the dose without checking with your care team, and ask them or a pharmacist whether another medicine could suit you better.

Seek urgent help if you have trouble breathing, are unusually hard to wake, faint, develop severe abdominal pain, or keep vomiting and can’t keep fluids down. What painkiller are you taking, and when does the nausea start?

I understand you’re waiting for home care. Please contact her doctor, nurse, or an urgent medical service **today** for advice and catheter replacement—don’t wait until tomorrow if you can get help sooner. She should be assessed within a day or two. Don’t try to reinsert the catheter yourself; keep her clean and dry, use absorbent pads, and note when she last passed urine.

Seek emergency care now for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or headache with weakness, confusion, fainting, vision or speech problems, fever and stiff neck, or after a head injury. If it’s new, worsening, frequent, or not improving, contact a healthcare professional.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Severe abdominal pain, fainting, pale skin, and reduced responsiveness are an emergency—don’t wait or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available.
