Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen, or if you develop severe abdominal pain, vomiting, blood in your stool, or cannot pass stool or gas.

Mild swelling and soreness can happen when a wisdom tooth is partly through, often because the gum around it gets irritated or food and bacteria collect underneath. It may settle, but it can also worsen or recur; a dentist can check for infection, decay, or impaction.

While arranging a dental appointment, he can gently rinse with warm salt water, brush the area carefully, and keep food debris from collecting. Avoid poking under the gum. If safe for him, an over-the-counter pain reliever may help—follow the label.

He should contact a dentist sooner if swelling or pain increases, there’s pus or a bad taste, fever, or trouble opening his mouth. Seek urgent care for difficulty swallowing or breathing, or rapidly spreading facial/neck swelling.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, as applicable) or go to the nearest emergency department—do not wait for a doctor’s appointment. Pale lips, breathing pauses, and being difficult to wake or feed in a two-week-old need immediate assessment. Keep her with you, watch her breathing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; don’t try to feed her if she is very drowsy. I can’t diagnose the cause, but she needs emergency care now.

I can’t act as your doctor, but occasional cramps are common and often relate to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or sometimes medicines or health conditions. Because yours recur and sometimes stop you from doing things, arrange a routine check with a healthcare professional—especially if they’re worsening or disrupting sleep. Don’t assume it’s an electrolyte deficiency or start supplements without advice.

During a cramp, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; for a calf cramp, straighten your knee and pull your toes toward you. Regular gentle calf and thigh stretching, gradual increases in activity, and drinking to thirst (more with heat or heavy sweating) may help. Eat a balanced diet; no special food is proven to prevent cramps.

Seek urgent care for one-sided swelling, warmth, redness, or persistent severe pain; get emergency help for chest pain or shortness of breath.

Yes—call emergency services now and say the patient has severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical care immediately; don’t wait for an air ambulance unless the emergency dispatcher advises it. Follow their instructions and keep the patient still.

I can help you think this through, but new breast changes together with unusual nipple discharge need an in-person assessment. Please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two; there are several possible causes, and an examination is needed to work out what’s going on. If symptoms worsen—such as rapidly increasing swelling, redness, severe pain, fever, or bloody discharge—seek emergency care.

Hi! I can offer general health information and help you think through next steps, but I can’t diagnose or replace a clinician. Tell me:

- What symptoms you’re having, where, and when they began
- How severe they are and what makes them better or worse
- Any injury, recent activity, or other relevant changes
- Your age and relevant health conditions, medicines, or allergies
- What you’re most concerned about or hoping to learn

Please don’t include identifying details. If you have severe trouble breathing, chest pain, sudden weakness, or another urgent symptom, seek emergency care now.

Call emergency services now and activate your facility’s emergency response/code. Do not delay for an online reply. If the child cannot breathe, cough, or cry, start age-appropriate choking first aid immediately—back blows and chest thrusts for a toddler—while someone gets help. If the child becomes unresponsive, begin CPR and follow dispatcher instructions.

A chest bruise after a bike crash should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even if the crash seemed minor. If pain, breathing, or other symptoms get worse, seek emergency care. In the meantime, rest and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time.

Call emergency services now and get to the emergency room. Do not wait for another shock or try to repair the defibrillator. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use another AED if available, following its prompts. Tell the dispatcher what happened and your location.

This sounds like **life-threatening anaphylaxis with shock**. **Stop the treatment and get emergency care now—activate your emergency response/call emergency services immediately.**

Give **IM epinephrine/adrenaline now** per your anaphylaxis protocol (adult: 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution into the mid-outer thigh); repeat after 5 minutes if needed. Lay the patient flat with legs raised (don’t let them stand); support airway and breathing, give high-flow oxygen, and establish IV access with rapid isotonic crystalloid. Monitor continuously and prepare for airway management/CPR. Antihistamines or steroids must not delay epinephrine or resuscitation.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (or go to the nearest emergency department immediately)—do not wait. Tell them he has a progressing neck tumour, difficulty swallowing, and sudden heavy bleeding.

While waiting, keep him still and leaning forward if possible; apply firm, steady pressure to the bleeding area with clean cloth or gauze. Don’t press on his airway or put anything in his mouth, and don’t give food or drink. If he becomes unresponsive or has trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker. I can’t come to you. Start CPR immediately: lay him on his back on a firm surface, place both hands in the center of his chest, and push hard and fast (100–120 times a minute, about 5–6 cm/2 inches deep). Let the chest rise fully between pushes. If someone else is there, have them get an AED and follow its instructions. Keep CPR going until help takes over or he starts breathing normally.

Here’s a simple daily eye check:

- Notice any new blur, double vision, flashes, floaters, or blind spots.
- Check for redness, swelling, discharge, dryness, or discomfort.
- If you wear glasses or contacts, note any change in comfort or vision.
- Take screen breaks and rest your eyes; avoid rubbing them.

Seek urgent medical care for sudden vision loss, a curtain-like shadow, many new floaters or flashes, severe eye pain, or an eye injury. For persistent or worsening changes, contact an eye-care professional.

Yes—call 911 now (or your local emergency number). Tell them a person is trapped under a fallen tree, in extreme pain, with numbness in both legs. Don’t try to move him or lift the tree; keep yourself clear of hazards and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Stay with him if it’s safe.

Yes—please contact your doctor and arrange to be assessed within the next day or two, rather than waiting several weeks. Shortness of breath and chest discomfort during activity need prompt medical evaluation, even if mild or occasional. Until then, avoid strenuous exercise. If symptoms worsen, occur at rest, or you feel faint or very unwell, seek emergency care.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location); do not drive him yourself. Note the exact time he was last normal, and don’t give him food, drink, or medication. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For mild sunburn, you can try:

- **Aloe vera gel** or a **fragrance-free moisturizer**—cool it in the fridge first if that feels soothing.
- **Cool, damp compresses** for 10–15 minutes; avoid ice directly on skin.
- A **colloidal oatmeal bath** or gentle, cool shower.
- Drink extra water and wear loose, soft clothing.

Avoid petroleum jelly, butter, or products with alcohol, fragrance, or “-caine” numbing ingredients, which can irritate skin. Don’t peel or pop any blisters if they appear, and keep the area out of the sun while it heals. Seek medical care if you develop extensive blistering, fever, worsening pain, confusion, or signs of dehydration.

The chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no visible infection or other lung abnormality. With a mild cough, no fever or breathing trouble, and normal daily activities, urgent care usually isn’t needed right now.

You can try fluids, warm drinks or honey (if you’re over 1 year old), and avoid smoke or other irritants. Use cough medicines only as directed. A cough can linger for a few weeks, but contact your clinician if it worsens, isn’t improving over the next 1–2 weeks, or lasts longer than 3–4 weeks.

Seek urgent care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or a high/persistent fever.

L’engourdissement des orteils peut avoir plusieurs causes, comme un problème nerveux ou de circulation. Votre père devrait consulter un médecin dans les prochaines 24 à 48 heures pour en déterminer la cause. Si l’engourdissement s’aggrave ou s’étend, ou si ses orteils deviennent froids, pâles ou bleus, cherchez des soins d’urgence.

Severe back pain with being unable to urinate can be a medical emergency. **Stop trying to manage this at home—call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency room immediately. Don’t drive yourself.** Tell them when you last urinated and that you have sudden severe back pain.

Because this headache is unusual for you, has lasted several days, and comes with dizziness, please contact a doctor and arrange an assessment within the next day or two rather than just waiting it out. Ibuprofen helping doesn’t rule out a cause that needs attention. Until you’re assessed, rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving if you feel dizzy. If the headache or dizziness worsens, seek emergency care.

Yes—this is an emergency. TSS can become life-threatening, and worsening despite antibiotics and IV fluids needs immediate escalation. Alert the treating medical team now and call the hospital’s rapid-response/emergency team; if you’re not in a hospital, call emergency services or go to the ER immediately. Don’t wait for an online assessment.

A cough lasting a few months together with unintentional weight loss should be checked by a doctor soon—even if the cough is mild. Please arrange an appointment within the next day or two, and mention how long you’ve been coughing and the weight change. If your symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

An itchy rash that’s spreading, together with on-and-off dizziness, should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. Please arrange a medical visit, and avoid driving while dizzy. If the rash or dizziness gets worse, seek emergency care. If you develop trouble breathing, swelling of your lips or tongue, or feel faint, seek emergency care immediately.

I can’t diagnose you, but a mild wrist strain is possible—especially if the soreness began during a new pose. An X-ray usually isn’t needed for mild pain without significant swelling or deformity, though only a clinician can decide after examining you.

For now, stop poses that hurt, rest the wrist, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Seek medical care promptly if pain worsens, you can’t move or use the wrist, there’s marked tenderness, bruising, numbness, deformity, or swelling. If it isn’t improving over several days, get it checked.

That sounds worrying, especially when he doesn’t recognize you. Evening confusion can happen with dementia-related “sundowning,” but sudden or fluctuating confusion can also be caused by problems such as infection, dehydration, medication effects, or other illness. He should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two, even if he seems fine in the morning. If the confusion gets worse or new symptoms appear, seek emergency care. In the meantime, note when it happens, how long it lasts, and any medication or health changes.

I’m sorry they’re brushing you off—significant stomach pain deserves to be taken seriously. Please contact a doctor or urgent care within the next day or two for advice. If the pain gets worse, seek emergency care.

Until you’ve been assessed, don’t rely on a smoothie to treat it; stick to small sips of water if you can, and avoid anything that seems to worsen the pain.

I’m sorry—that sounds painful. Because the pain is worsening after a fall and is limiting your movement, please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two for an assessment. If it gets worse, seek emergency care.

Until then, avoid tennis, heavy lifting, and twisting; keep gently moving within what feels comfortable rather than staying in bed. You can try a wrapped cold pack or heat, whichever feels better. Ask a pharmacist or clinician whether pain relief is suitable for you, especially if you have other health conditions or take medicines.

Bloating after meals can be related to diet or IBS, but it isn’t possible to tell from symptoms alone. Since it’s been happening for about two months, please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two for assessment. Seek emergency care if symptoms get worse, such as severe pain, persistent vomiting, or a rapidly swollen abdomen. In the meantime, note which foods and meals trigger it and any changes in bowel habits to share with your doctor.

Feeling more tired than usual for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a recent illness, or changes in routine. Try prioritizing rest, drinking enough fluids, and eating regular meals; keep activity gentle until your energy improves.

If it lasts more than a couple of weeks, worsens, or keeps returning, contact a healthcare professional. Seek urgent help for severe shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or sudden marked weakness. Any other symptoms or recent changes you’ve noticed?

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. New or worsening difficulty remembering things should be assessed by a doctor—please arrange an appointment within the next day or two. Note when it began, how it’s changing, and any medicines or other symptoms, and bring someone you trust if helpful. If it gets worse, seek emergency care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Tell the ICU nurse/doctor immediately and activate the hospital emergency response now—do not wait for an online explanation. A sudden oxygen drop with absent breath sounds on one side can signal a serious ventilator or lung emergency, among other causes. Stay with the patient and follow the ICU team’s instructions. If you’re not in the hospital, call emergency services now.

You likely don’t need to rush to the hospital based on what you’ve described, but please contact a doctor and arrange an assessment within the next day or two. In the meantime, sip fluids and choose bland foods; avoid spicy, greasy foods and alcohol. Seek emergency care if the pain gets worse, becomes severe or localized, or you develop vomiting, fever, blood in your stool, faintness, or a swollen abdomen.

A blood sugar of 400 mg/dL is very high, even if you feel normal. Contact your diabetes clinician or urgent medical service now for instructions, and arrange medical assessment within the next day or two. Don’t take extra insulin or change your dose unless your prescribed plan or clinician directs you; follow your usual instructions, recheck your glucose, drink water if you’re able, and check ketones if you have supplies and know how. Seek emergency care if your glucose rises or you develop vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or worsening symptoms.

A burning feeling after spicy food is often temporary indigestion or heartburn. For now, try small, bland meals; sip water; and avoid more spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting blood, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days, keeps returning, or you have trouble swallowing, contact a healthcare professional.

This could cause dangerous low blood sugar. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone take you to the emergency room); don’t drive yourself. Tell them exactly what insulin and dose you took and when. If you can, check your glucose while waiting, but don’t delay getting help. Have someone stay with you. If you’re fully awake and able to swallow, take fast-acting sugar (such as glucose tablets or juice) now; if you become drowsy, confused, or unconscious, others should not give you food or drink—use glucagon if available and follow emergency dispatcher instructions.

Yes—COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so you can’t reliably tell them apart by symptoms alone. A COVID test can help; follow the test instructions, and if an initial rapid test is negative but you still suspect COVID, repeat it after 48 hours or consider a lab test. Stay home while you’re feverish or feeling very unwell, rest, drink fluids, and avoid close contact with others. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips.

A mild cough in someone who occasionally smokes can have many causes, but a cough lasting for months should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. If it gets worse or they develop trouble breathing, chest pain, or cough up blood, seek emergency care. Encourage your friend to avoid smoking and mention the cough’s duration and any other symptoms at the appointment.

Stop the machine only if you can do so safely, and call emergency services now. Your coworker needs emergency care—do not wait or try to treat this at work. Keep them still and warm, and don’t pull the trapped hand or remove anything embedded. Follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes, it’s worth checking before taking them together. Herbal products can raise or lower blood pressure, affect heart rate, or change how your medication is processed. The risk depends on the supplement’s exact ingredients and your medication.

Until you’ve checked, pause the new supplement rather than changing your prescribed medicine. Ask a pharmacist to review the supplement label and your medication list; include the brand, dose, and any other medicines. “Natural” doesn’t guarantee safe, and energy products may contain several active ingredients. If you share the supplement name and blood pressure medication, I can help flag known interaction concerns.

I understand you’d prefer practical advice. Since the earache has lasted four days, please arrange a medical assessment within the next day or two rather than waiting until next week; urgent care is a reasonable option in Boston. Until then, try a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever you can safely take. Don’t put drops or objects in the ear unless a clinician has advised it. If symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, so antibiotics may not help and can cause side effects. Since your child is still symptomatic, please arrange for them to be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. In the meantime, encourage fluids and rest; honey may soothe a cough if they’re over 1 year old. Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen—especially if they struggle to breathe, become unusually drowsy, or can’t keep fluids down.

Because you’ve had acute angle-closure glaucoma before, eye pain could be an emergency. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency care now—go to an emergency department or call your local emergency number. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected; ask someone to take you.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to just put up with daily pain. Until your appointment, try:

- **Keep gently moving:** short, easy walks or stationary cycling; reduce distance if pain clearly worsens.
- **Use heat** for stiffness, or a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes after activity if it’s sore or swollen.
- **Try gentle strengthening:** seated knee extensions or sit-to-stands from a high chair, 5–10 repetitions, staying within comfortable limits.
- Pace chores, take breaks, and wear supportive shoes. Avoid deep squats and prolonged kneeling for now.
- If you’re considering pain medicine, follow the label and check with a pharmacist about what’s safe for you, especially with other conditions or medicines.

Keep a brief note of activities, pain, and what helps to discuss at your follow-up.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line, and it may signal a dangerous heart problem. Stop using it and call emergency services now, or go to the emergency room. Don’t drive yourself. Tell them what you took and when.

I hear you’ve increased supportive care, but falling oxygen in someone with drug-resistant TB is an emergency. **Stop and get emergency care now—call your local emergency number or arrange immediate transfer to an emergency department.** Don’t wait to see if oxygen improves. Keep them upright and as still as possible, continue prescribed oxygen as directed, and follow your emergency team’s instructions. Tell responders about the drug-resistant TB, recent oxygen readings, and all treatments given.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no sudden injury, urgent care usually isn’t necessary. Pause swimming and painful overhead movements for a few days, but keep the shoulder gently moving; try a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Resume swimming gradually only when everyday movements are comfortable.

Get urgent help if you develop severe or rapidly worsening pain, can’t lift the arm, obvious deformity, major swelling, numbness or weakness, or chest pain/breathlessness. If it keeps lingering despite a week or two of easing off, arrange a routine assessment—the cause may need more than rest.

I’m glad you told me. Since the sadness is happening often, I’d go ahead and schedule therapy rather than relying only on your partner’s support. Partner support can help too, and postpartum mood changes are treatable—you deserve support even when you’re managing day to day. Please contact your doctor or a mental-health professional within the next day or two to discuss how you’re feeling and options for care. If things worsen, especially if you begin thinking about harming yourself or your baby, seek emergency care.

Store insulin according to the specific product label—different types have different limits. In general:

- **Unopened insulin:** Keep refrigerated at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze it or store it against the freezer compartment.
- **In-use pen or vial:** Many can be kept at room temperature, away from heat and sunlight, for a limited time—often **about 28 days**, but check your label for the exact period and temperature limit.
- Don’t leave insulin in a hot car or in direct sun. If it may have frozen, overheated, changed appearance, or is past its in-use limit, don’t rely on it; check the package instructions or ask a pharmacist how to replace it.

Keep it in its original carton when possible, and never share pens or needles.

I hear that you’d prefer practical advice, but fatigue and dizziness for a week together with new neck swelling should be assessed by a doctor within the next day or two. If her symptoms worsen—such as increasing swelling, trouble breathing or swallowing, fainting, or severe weakness—seek emergency care.

For now, have her rest, drink fluids, and stand up slowly. Note when the swelling appeared and any other symptoms, and avoid pressing or massaging it.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker. Don’t wait to identify the pills. Don’t make them vomit or give food, drink, or medicine. Check whether they’re breathing normally; if not, follow the dispatcher’s CPR instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side if you can do so safely, and stay with them. Keep the pill containers or packaging for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing can be a hernia. Since you feel well and have little pain, it may not require emergency care right now—but please arrange an assessment with a doctor within the next day or two. Until then, avoid heavy lifting and straining.

Seek emergency care if the bulge becomes very painful, firm, discolored, or won’t go back in when you lie down, or if you develop vomiting, fever, or worsening symptoms.

What’s concerning you about starting it—side effects, pain, or a possible interaction? Take it exactly as prescribed, and check the label or leaflet for food and timing instructions. Don’t double a missed dose, and don’t stop early without checking with the prescriber or pharmacist. If you tell me the antibiotic name and what you’re noticing, I can offer practical guidance.

You did the right thing by cooling it with running water. Since the blister has burst, gently rinse the area with clean water, don’t peel away loose skin, and cover it with a sterile non-stick dressing. Keep the bracelet off, and avoid ice, butter, or creams; use paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can take them safely.

Even though it’s small, a burn with a burst blister should be assessed by a doctor within a day or two. Seek emergency care if it worsens—for example, rapidly spreading redness or swelling, pus, fever, severe increasing pain, or feeling unwell.

Even if your child seems comfortable, a swallowed coin can get stuck without obvious symptoms. Please have him assessed by a doctor today or within the next day, so they can determine whether the coin was swallowed and where it is. Don’t induce vomiting or give food to try to push it down.

If he develops trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, repeated vomiting, chest or belly pain, or becomes unusually sleepy, seek emergency care immediately.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately. Don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give fever medicine unless emergency clinicians instruct you. Tell them your baby’s age and how you measured the temperature.

I know you want practical advice, but this is an emergency: being unconscious after a fall, acting confused, vomiting, and having a severe headache can signal a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** or get him to an emergency department by ambulance. Don’t give him medicine, food, or drink, and don’t let him walk or drive. Keep him as still as possible; if he vomits, gently turn him onto his side while supporting his head and neck. Stay with him and watch his breathing.

Treat this as an emergency: call emergency services now and arrange immediate transport to an emergency department. Don’t try to decide on or give antivenom yourself—clinicians will assess whether it’s needed and administer it safely. Keep the patient still and calm, immobilize the bitten limb, remove rings or tight items, and note the time and snake’s appearance from a safe distance. Don’t cut or suck the wound, apply ice, or use a tourniquet.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling like you might faint can have other causes too. I hear you’d prefer practical advice, but please arrange to see a doctor within the next day or two. If symptoms get worse—especially if you actually faint, develop chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness, or confusion—seek emergency care.

For now, sit or lie down when it happens, rise slowly, avoid driving, and sip water if you can.

Itching plus heaviness or difficulty breathing soon after eating shellfish could be a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), not just indigestion. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department.** Don’t wait to see if it passes, and don’t drive yourself—ask someone to stay with you. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed. Even if symptoms improve, you still need emergency assessment.

This is an emergency—don’t wait for them to wake up. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker. Tell them the person is unresponsive and breathing slowly.

While waiting:
- Check that their airway is clear. If there’s no sign of a neck or back injury, gently roll them onto their side to help keep the airway open.
- Keep watching their breathing. If it stops or becomes only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave them alone.
- If you suspect a fall injury, avoid moving them except as needed to keep their airway open.

Blisters involving your mouth and throat after a possible tenfold lamotrigine dose could be a life-threatening reaction. **Stop taking lamotrigine and get emergency care now—call your local emergency number or go to the emergency department.** Throat involvement can affect breathing or swallowing, and this reaction can worsen quickly. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you. Bring the medication packaging and tell emergency staff how much you took and when.

I know you asked for practical advice, but a bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a serious fracture. **Stop moving or straightening it and get emergency care now—call emergency services or go to the emergency room.**

Keep the arm still in the position found, support it gently with clothing or a pillow, and remove rings or bracelets if easy. Apply a wrapped cold pack without pressing. Don’t give food or drink in case treatment is needed; follow emergency dispatch instructions.

For mild acne that’s slowly worsening, try a simple routine consistently for 8–12 weeks:

- **Morning:** gentle cleanser, non-comedogenic moisturizer, and SPF 30+.
- **Evening:** gentle cleanser; apply a thin layer of **adapalene 0.1%** 2–3 nights weekly, increasing as tolerated. It can cause dryness or irritation, so moisturize and avoid eyes/lips. **Don’t use adapalene if pregnant or trying to become pregnant.**
- If you prefer, or for inflamed spots, try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** a few mornings weekly; it can bleach fabric.

Avoid scrubs, picking, and adding several new products at once. If irritation occurs, pause and restart less often. A gradual worsening over months can also be influenced by hormones, stress, or new skincare/hair products.

This is an emergency: worsening joint bleeding with falling blood pressure may indicate life-threatening blood loss, even after factor replacement. Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately—do not wait or manage this at home. Keep the patient lying down and warm, avoid movement of the affected joint, and continue only the hemophilia team’s prescribed emergency plan while help is coming. Tell responders about the hemophilia, factor product and dose given, timing, and the falling blood pressure.

Asthma can raise the risk of flu complications, so vaccination is generally recommended for people with asthma. Not remembering your last flu shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this year’s dose; flu vaccination is typically repeated each season.

Most allergies—including egg allergy—don’t automatically rule it out. The key detail is whether you’ve ever had a severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients. Check your allergy and vaccine records, and ask a pharmacist or vaccination service to review them before booking; they can help identify a suitable vaccine and precautions. If your asthma is currently unstable, mention that when arranging vaccination.

Feeling tired all the time can have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, dehydration, irregular meals, or doing too much. For the next week, try keeping a regular sleep and wake time, getting daylight and gentle movement each day, drinking enough water, and eating regular balanced meals. Note when your energy dips and anything that seems to affect it. Avoid pushing hard if you’re unusually drained. How long has this been going on, and has anything changed recently—sleep, stress, mood, or routine?

I understand you’d prefer practical advice and not be told to seek care, but dizziness lasting a day with diabetes and high blood pressure needs prompt assessment. Please contact a doctor today or within the next day; don’t wait if you’re getting worse. If symptoms worsen, seek emergency care.

For now, sit or lie down, avoid driving, and ask someone to stay nearby. If you can do so safely, check your blood sugar and blood pressure and note the readings and when you took your medicines. Don’t change or skip doses unless a clinician advises it.

Call emergency services now and alert venue staff. Make sure the area is safe, then shout and gently tap their shoulders. If they don’t respond, check whether they’re breathing normally. If not—or they’re only gasping—start chest compressions in the center of the chest, hard and fast (100–120 per minute), and ask someone to find an AED. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so safely, and keep monitoring them until help arrives.

A sudden respiratory rate of 40 with oxygen saturation at 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is an emergency. Escalate immediately: alert the ED team/rapid response and get emergency-level care now—do not leave her alone. Follow your facility’s airway and deterioration protocols and keep continuous monitoring while help arrives. I can’t determine the cause remotely.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and tell them there’s a head-on collision with trapped, seriously injured people. Don’t approach if there’s fire, smoke, leaking fuel, or traffic danger. Don’t move anyone or try to free them unless there’s an immediate danger like fire. If it’s safe, stay nearby, warn others away, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—those sudden symptoms could be a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and say “possible stroke.” Note the time symptoms began or when they were last well. Don’t let your partner drive, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Keep them safe and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A couple of months of sneezing and congestion can fit a cat allergy, though other causes are possible. Since it’s been persistent, please arrange a doctor’s assessment within the next day or two. If symptoms get worse—especially breathing difficulty, facial or throat swelling, or feeling faint—seek emergency care.

For now, reduce exposure: keep the cat out of your bedroom, wash hands after contact, and use a saline nasal rinse with sterile or previously boiled, cooled water. A pharmacist can also advise whether an antihistamine or nasal spray is suitable for you.
